That is very hard to understand, yet we have good reason to accept it: the evidence and rigorous theory point that way, and the phenomena are so remote from everyday experience that we must stretch concepts drawn from ordinary objects far beyond their home territory. We have good reason to believe both that wave–particle duality is real and that we will not fully grasp how it works.

Reasoning to a purely actual, absolutely simple cause of all things takes us even farther from everyday experience than physics does — to the most fundamental level of reality. Our concepts and language must be stretched to their absolute limit, so it would be surprising if the conclusions were *not* hard to comprehend. Reason itself thus tells us that there is a level of reality that reason can only partly understand. Feser notes that much more will be said in the chapter on the divine attributes, but that enough has been said to show that proving an absolutely simple cause is proving God.

The structure of the reply is worth noting. Feser is not saying ‘it is mysterious, so it must be true.’ He is saying that the argument gives us reasons to accept the conclusion, and that the conclusion's difficulty is not a counter-reason, because difficulty is exactly what we should predict in this domain.
summary.takeaway: The difficulty of understanding a simple being whose attributes are one is predicted by the argument itself, just as the difficulty of wave–particle duality is predicted by how far physics reaches beyond everyday experience.
summary.deepDive:
The key distinction in this section is between what is **hard to comprehend** and what is **incoherent**. They are easy to confuse, and much criticism of divine simplicity trades on the confusion.

An incoherent claim contradicts itself: a square circle, a married bachelor. We can see that it cannot be true. A hard-to-comprehend claim is one we cannot picture or fully grasp, though nothing shows it contradicts itself. Modern science is full of these. Light and electrons behave in some experiments like particles and in others like waves. Space-time can be curved. No one can form a satisfying mental image of these facts, yet the evidence and the mathematics compel them.

Why are such truths hard to grasp? Feser's answer is illuminating. Our concepts are formed from everyday experience of medium-sized objects — balls, ripples, tables. When we apply them to things very remote from that experience, we have to stretch them far beyond their home territory, and they strain. The farther from ordinary experience, the more they strain. So difficulty is not a sign of error; in remote domains it is exactly what a correct account should produce.

Now place the One on that scale. Physics describes the structure of the material world. The Neo-Platonic argument reaches beyond all material structure to the absolutely simple, purely actual ground of the existence of everything, physics included. That is the most remote domain there is. So if our account of it felt easy and familiar, *that* would be suspicious. Feser draws a striking conclusion: reason itself shows that there is a level of reality reason can only partly comprehend.

Note what Feser is *not* saying. He is not appealing to mystery as a trump card, as if ‘it's a mystery’ settled every objection. The argument supplies positive reasons for each attribute; the analogy only answers the specific charge that the conclusion is too strange to be true. Nor is he saying God is wholly unknowable. We know that the One exists, much about what it is not (not composite, changeable, material, or abstract), and, by analogy, something of what it is. Chapter 6 returns to this under the heading of divine incomprehensibility.

This section defends the coherence of **steps 36–37** against the objection ‘I can't make sense of that.’ The usual confusion is to treat ‘I can't picture it’ as if it meant ‘it's contradictory.’

checks.q: A critic says, ‘I can't picture a being whose power is identical to its intellect, so it can't exist.’ Which reply best reflects Feser's reasoning?
options: Then the argument must be unsound
Picturing it becomes easy once one has faith
Physics shows that God has parts after all
Inability to picture it is expected when concepts are stretched far beyond everyday experience, and it is not evidence of contradiction
checks.explanation: Feser compares the case to wave–particle duality: hard to grasp, yet well supported, because the domain is remote from ordinary experience.

checks.q: What does Feser conclude reason tells us about the most fundamental level of reality?
options: That there is a level of reality reason can only partially comprehend
That reason can comprehend it completely
That reason can say nothing at all about it
That only physics can describe it
checks.explanation: Reason both proves the simple cause exists and shows why we should find it hard to understand.

summary.heading: The formal statement
summary.body:
Feser then restates the argument in thirty-eight numbered steps. Steps 1–9 establish that each composite thing of our experience presupposes, here and now, an absolutely simple cause. Steps 10–13 prove that there can be only one such cause; 14–19 that it is immutable, without beginning or end, and eternal; 20–21 that it is uncaused; 22–29 that it is a mind; 30–32 that it is the ultimate cause of everything other than itself; 33–35 that it is purely actual and therefore perfect, omnipotent, fully good, and omniscient; and 36–38 that such a cause is God. Every step, with its justification, appears in the Argument section of this module.

Three things are worth noticing about the formal version. First, its premises are few and do almost all the work: that things are composite (step 1), that composites exist only while their parts are combined (2), that combination needs a concurrent cause (3), that the resulting regress is hierarchical and must terminate (7), and that only the simple could terminate it (8). Second, most of Stage 2 applies a single pattern — if the cause had X it would have parts, it has no parts, so it lacks X — to change (14), beginning and end (16), being caused (20), and potentiality (33). Third, two stretches borrow from elsewhere: steps 22–29 adopt Vallicella's classification to show the cause is a mind, and step 35 imports chapter 1's derivation of perfection, omnipotence, goodness, and omniscience from pure actuality.

The practical upshot for a critic is clear. To resist the conclusion, one must reject a specific premise. Merely asserting that the cause need not be God, or that the chain might go back forever in time, engages none of them.
summary.takeaway: The thirty-eight steps rest on a handful of premises about composition and hierarchy, plus one repeated move — ‘if it had X it would have parts’ — so a critic must reject a specific premise rather than the conclusion in general.
summary.deepDive:
A formal statement is a tool for checking an argument, and learning to read one is a skill. Here is how to approach Feser's thirty-eight steps.

**Sort premises from inferences.** Premises are claims defended on their own (steps 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 23, 25, 27, 33, 35, 37). Inferences follow from earlier steps (4, 5, 9, 12, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34, 36, 38). If the premises are true and each inference is valid, the conclusion must be true. So the only honest ways to resist are to deny a premise or to show that an inference does not follow.

**Find the load-bearing premises.** In Stage 1 they are steps 2, 3, 7, and 8. Step 3 (composition needs a concurrent cause) is where the ‘further part,’ ‘brute fact,’ and ‘laws of nature’ objections attack. Step 7 (the hierarchy must terminate) rests on chapter 1's analysis of per se series. In Stage 2, the most contestable are step 22 (is the fourfold classification exhaustive?) and step 35 (which depends on chapter 1).

**Notice what survives if one part fails.** Suppose someone showed that step 22's list is incomplete. That would weaken the direct argument that the One is a mind. But Stage 1 would stand, and so would the attributes derived from simplicity: uniqueness, immutability, eternity, uncausedness, pure actuality. And through pure actuality and proportionate causality, chapter 1 supplies another route to intellect. The argument is not a house of cards in which every step holds up every other.

**Try an exercise.** Pick any premise. Write the strongest objection you can think of in one sentence. Then find Feser's reply in this module (each step's ‘challenge’ and ‘answer’ fields will help). If you can't find a reply, you have located a point worth pressing — which is exactly how Feser wants the arguments to be engaged.

The usual confusions are two. Some think thirty-eight steps means thirty-eight independent assumptions; in fact half the steps are inferences, and many premises are applications of one idea. Others think one can refute the argument by attacking the plausibility of the conclusion — ‘there's no God, so something must be wrong.’ That begs the question. Feser presents these as demonstrations: to reject the conclusion, show which step fails.

checks.q: Which steps are the load-bearing premises of Stage 1?
options: Steps 10, 11, and 14
Steps 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8
Steps 22, 23, and 25
Steps 35 and 37 only
checks.explanation: Stage 1 moves from composition (1–3) through the hierarchical regress (6–7) to the necessity of a simple terminus (8).

checks.q: Which pattern generates most of Stage 2's attributes?
options: Whatever humans have, God has more of
Whatever is observed must have a cause
If the simple cause had X, it would have parts; it has no parts; so it lacks X
Whatever is possible must be actual
checks.explanation: Applied to change (14), beginning and end (16), being caused (20), and potentiality (33).

checks.q: If a critic showed that step 22's classification is not exhaustive, what would remain standing?
options: Nothing: the whole argument would collapse
Only the conclusion that God is a mind
Only step 38
Stage 1's conclusion and the attributes derived from simplicity, such as uniqueness, immutability, eternity, and pure actuality
checks.explanation: Only the direct elimination argument for intellect would be affected, and pure actuality offers another route to it via chapter 1.

summary.heading: Objections shared with the Aristotelian proof
summary.body:
Several objections to this argument are the same ones raised against the Aristotelian proof, and the same replies apply.

- **“A first cause needn't be God.”** Detailed criticisms of particular attribute-derivations are postponed to chapter 6. But it is lazy simply to assert that a first cause need not be divine, because reasons have now been given for thinking it must be.
- **“It assumes the universe had a beginning.”** It does not. The chain of causes is traced not backward into the past but downward to the present moment.
- **“If everything has a cause, what caused God?”** The argument never says everything has a cause; it says whatever is *composite* has a cause. God is not an arbitrary exception. Only what is in some way composite needs, or even could have, a cause; something absolutely simple not only needs no cause but could not have one. Nor was this invented to dodge the objection; it was the Neo-Platonic tradition's view from the beginning. Far from being devastating, the objection simply misses the point.
- **Hume and quantum mechanics.** Appeals to these against the premise that composites need causes fare no better here than they did against the Aristotelian proof, and the reader is referred back to chapter 1.

What unites these replies is a single diagnosis: each objection attacks a claim the argument does not make. It does not claim the universe began; it does not claim everything has a cause; it does not leave the nature of the first cause unaddressed. That is why Feser's advice is to review chapter 1's replies, since the same misreadings recur.
summary.takeaway: The stock objections — ‘needn't be God,’ ‘assumes a beginning,’ ‘what caused God?,’ Hume, quantum mechanics — all target claims the Neo-Platonic proof never makes.
summary.deepDive:
The most famous of these objections is ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ It is worth seeing exactly why it misfires here, because the Neo-Platonic proof shows the reason more clearly than any other.

Start with the difference between two principles:

1. Everything has a cause.
2. Whatever is composite has a cause of its composition.

The objection attacks principle 1. The argument uses principle 2. The difference is like the difference between ‘all geometrical figures have three sides’ and ‘all triangles have three sides’ — an analogy Feser uses in chapter 1. The second is true and says nothing about circles.

But the Neo-Platonic proof goes further than merely *restricting* the principle. It explains *why* the restriction is natural. What is it to cause something's existence? It is to account for the union of its parts — pieces, form and matter, essence and existence. A simple being has nothing to be united. So there is nothing for a cause to do. As Feser puts it, the simple not only needs no cause; it *could not* have one. God is not an exception to the rule; he is outside its scope by the rule's own content.

Critics sometimes reply that this is ad hoc — invented to dodge the question. Chapter 1 gives three responses, and they apply here: even if the motive were suspect, that wouldn't make the claim false (to argue otherwise is ad hominem); historically, the tradition held this view from the start — Feser says the Neo-Platonic tradition always had it in mind; and the principle follows from the analysis of composition independently of any theological agenda.

On **Hume**: imagining a chair popping into existence without imagining its cause is not imagining it with *no* cause. And even a chair that popped into existence would, at every moment afterward, have its parts united — so the here-and-now question would remain. On **quantum mechanics**: indeterminism at most shows some events lack deterministic causes, not that composite things exist with no ground of their composition.

This section defends **steps 2–3 and 20–21**. The usual confusion is to think the argument is special pleading. Special pleading exempts a case arbitrarily; here the exemption is the principle's own content. And notice: the universe cannot take God's place as an uncaused thing, because it is massively composite.

checks.q: Feser says God has no cause not because he is an arbitrary exception but because…
options: only what is composite needs, or even could have, a cause
God chose not to have one
God is too old to have been caused
the universe is his cause
checks.explanation: The exemption follows from the principle's content: a simple being has nothing to be united.

checks.q: Someone says the ‘composite’ restriction was invented to dodge ‘What caused God?’. Which reply fits the chapter?
options: Feser admits it is ad hoc but harmless
The Neo-Platonic tradition held this from the beginning, and the restriction follows naturally from what it is to be caused
The objection is correct but irrelevant
God does have a cause, namely himself
checks.explanation: Feser stresses the historical point and the principled character of the restriction; self-causation is incoherent.

checks.q: Why does the argument survive the hypothesis that the universe is past-eternal?
options: Because Feser proves that the universe began
Because eternal things need no cause
It traces causes here and now to a simple cause, not backward to a first moment
Because Stage 2 doesn't depend on Stage 1
checks.explanation: The regress is one of present dependence; the age of the universe is irrelevant.

summary.heading: Could some part of the composite do the unifying?
summary.body:
The objections that target what is distinctive about this proof question its assumption that a composite's parts must be unified by something *external*. Why not say instead that some part of the thing unifies the rest, or that the unity is just an irreducible fact?

Following Vallicella, Feser argues that neither suggestion makes sense. Take a thing made of parts A and B. If we say some further part C unites them, we must ask what unites C with A and B. Positing a part D only moves the question back another step, and the same question recurs for every new part we add. Rather than solving the problem of A and B's unity, we have multiplied it.

The deeper problem is that a unifier which is itself one of the items to be unified cannot explain their unity. Suppose C were a kind of metaphysical glue. For C to do its job, C must itself be joined to A and to B; but that joining is exactly the sort of fact we were trying to explain. So either some further item joins C to them — and the question recurs — or the joining of C to A and B is left unexplained, in which case we might as well have left the joining of A and B unexplained in the first place. Either way, positing C adds nothing.

The lesson generalizes. Whatever does the unifying cannot be one more member of the collection it unifies. It must stand outside that collection, which is why the argument looks for an external cause, and ultimately for something that is not a collection at all.
summary.takeaway: No part of a composite can explain the union of its parts, because that part would itself need to be united with the rest, launching a regress that multiplies the problem instead of solving it.
summary.deepDive:
This reply, which Feser draws from William Vallicella, has a long history. Philosophers will recognize its family resemblance to **Bradley's regress**, named after the British philosopher F. H. Bradley: if a relation R is needed to relate A and B, what relates R to A and to B? A second relation? Then what relates that one? (The comparison is the course's, not Feser's.)

Let's work through a concrete version. Two boards are glued together. Someone says, ‘The glue is what unifies them.’ Fine — at the level of carpentry, that is true. But the question the argument asks is more basic: what accounts for the union of the whole — boards plus glue — at this moment? If we answer ‘the glue,’ we have forgotten that the glue is one of the items whose union with the others is in question. The glue sticks to the boards only because of molecular bonds, which are further items, which must themselves be bound to the rest, and so on. Every new unifier we name is simply one more thing on the list of things to be unified.

This matters for an important case. On the Aristotelian view, a thing's **substantial form** does unify its matter from within: it is what makes this matter a dog rather than a heap of chemicals. Isn't that a ‘part’ unifying the other parts? It is — and the Neo-Platonic argument can accept it. What it denies is that this intrinsic unification is *self-sufficient*. Form and matter are two principles, and their union, as Feser argued earlier, needs a cause outside them. So intrinsic unifying principles are compatible with the argument; they just don't end the regress.

The usual confusion is to say, ‘The thing's structure or organization unifies it.’ But the structure is the arrangement of the parts — that is, the very unity to be explained. Naming it doesn't explain it.

This section defends **step 3**: composition requires a cause, and specifically one that is not simply another part of the composite. It prepares the ground for **step 8**: since no member of a collection can ground the collection's unity, the ultimate ground must be something that is not a collection of parts at all — something absolutely simple.

checks.q: Feser's reply to the suggestion that part C unites parts A and B is that…
options: C would have to be divine
no thing has more than two parts
C would be identical to A
we would then need to explain what unites C with A and B, and so on without end
checks.explanation: Each posited unifier is one more item needing to be unified; the regress multiplies the problem.

checks.q: An Aristotelian says a thing's substantial form unifies its matter. Is this the ‘further part’ solution Feser rejects?
options: Form does unify matter from within, but the union of form and matter still needs an external cause, so it doesn't end the regress
Yes, and Feser therefore rejects hylomorphism
No, because form is not a part in any sense
Yes, and it succeeds in ending the regress
checks.explanation: Intrinsic unifiers are compatible with the argument; they just aren't self-sufficient.

summary.heading: Could the unity be an irreducible or brute fact?
summary.body:
The other suggestion is that the union of A and B is simply an irreducible fact about the thing. What would that mean? If it means the composite itself causes A and B to be united, then it would be both the cause and the effect of the same union — incoherent, since nothing can lift itself by its own bootstraps. If it means the union has no cause at all — a brute fact — then the critic is not offering an alternative explanation, as promised, but no explanation.

Suppose the critic admits this and says he is simply suggesting there may be no explanation. As the Plotinus scholar Lloyd Gerson has pointed out, that is not a serious reply to the Neo-Platonic argument. Its defender can answer that an explanation *has* been given — the parts are joined by an absolutely simple cause — and the critic has offered no non-question-begging reason to reject it. Merely noting that one could refuse to explain is not an objection to an explanation already on the table.

It is worth separating what the critic is entitled to say from what he is not. He is entitled to ask for reasons to accept the Neo-Platonic explanation — and the chapter supplies them. He is not entitled to treat the bare possibility of there being no explanation as though it were a competing explanation, or as though it automatically cancelled the one on offer. A detective who has solved a case need not abandon the solution because someone points out that, conceivably, crimes might have no perpetrator.
summary.takeaway: Calling a composite's unity ‘irreducible’ either makes the composite its own cause (incoherent) or declares the unity a brute fact — which offers no explanation, and gives no reason to reject the explanation already on the table.
summary.deepDive:
This section turns on a dilemma, and the skill to learn is spotting both horns.

The critic says: ‘A composite's unity is just an irreducible fact about it.’ Ask what ‘irreducible’ means.

**Horn 1: the composite explains its own unity.** Then the composite is both the cause of its parts' union and the effect of that union. But its existence consists in that union, so it would have to exist in order to bring about the condition of its existing. That is the bootstrapping incoherence from earlier in the chapter.

**Horn 2: nothing explains it; it's a brute fact.** Then the critic has not offered an alternative explanation, as he claimed; he has offered none. Feser's point is sharp: the rival was advertised as another explanation, and it turns out to be the absence of one.

Suppose the critic accepts Horn 2 openly: ‘Maybe there just is no explanation.’ Here Feser cites Lloyd Gerson, a leading Plotinus scholar: this is not a serious reply. Why not? Consider an everyday parallel. Your car is running and a mechanic explains why: the fuel system, the ignition, the engine. You reply, ‘Maybe there's no explanation — maybe it's just running.’ You haven't refuted the mechanic. You've declined to engage him. The Neo-Platonist has offered an explanation: the parts are united by an absolutely simple cause. To reject it, the critic needs a reason that doesn't simply assume the conclusion he wants — a non-question-begging reason. ‘That would be God, and I don't believe in God’ is not such a reason.

Note what Feser does *not* need here. He doesn't need to prove that brute facts are impossible everywhere. That broader claim — the principle of sufficient reason — is defended in chapter 5. In this chapter, the point is dialectical: when an explanation is available and unrefuted, ‘maybe there's no explanation’ carries no weight against it.

This section defends **step 3** from the most common modern escape route. The usual confusion is to treat ‘brute fact’ as a neutral default, as though the burden fell entirely on the one offering an explanation. But refusing to explain is also a position, and it has to be argued for — especially when the refusal would have to extend to the existence of every composite thing.

checks.q: If ‘irreducible fact’ means the composite causes its own unity, what is wrong with it?
options: Nothing is wrong with it
It makes the composite both cause and effect of the same union, which is incoherent
It makes the composite absolutely simple
It proves the composite is eternal
checks.explanation: The composite's existence consists in the union, so it can't be what produces the union.

checks.q: What is Gerson's point, as Feser uses it?
options: Plotinus's own argument is invalid
Brute facts are common in science
‘Maybe there's no explanation’ is not a serious reply when an explanation has been offered and not refuted
Composite things have no real parts
checks.explanation: The defender has given an explanation; the critic owes a non-question-begging reason to reject it.

checks.q: Someone says, ‘Some facts are brute, so the unity of things could be one of them.’ Which reply best follows the chapter?
options: Brute facts are impossible by definition
The unity of things is a brute fact, but so is God
Brute facts occur only in quantum mechanics
Even granting that some facts might be brute, that gives no reason to reject the explanation actually offered; it merely declines to explain
checks.explanation: The chapter's reply is dialectical; the full defense of the PSR comes in chapter 5.

summary.heading: Could science and the laws of nature explain composition?
summary.body:
A final strategy grants that the cause of composition is external but denies that it must be divine: perhaps science explains why A and B are joined, by appeal to laws of atomic structure, molecular cohesion, and the like. Feser replies that this is not a real alternative. However laws of nature are understood (a topic he takes up in a later chapter), any law-based explanation leaves us with some further composite whose composition needs explaining. If it is a law that things of type A and type B combine under certain conditions, we must ask why A and B are governed by *that* law rather than another. A, B, and the law together form a new complex — one more instance of exactly what needed explaining — so the regress continues instead of ending.

In a footnote Feser adds that Aristotelians do not think of laws as external rulers at all; a law is shorthand for how a thing tends to behave given its substantial form. But that makes matters worse for the critic, since a substantial form is, together with prime matter, one of the two basic principles the thing is composed of. The operation of a law therefore *presupposes* the very composition it was supposed to explain. The only way to end the regress is with something absolutely simple, and that, for the reasons given, cannot be anything less than divine.

In short, a law can describe how composition happens at a given level, but it cannot be what makes composite things — laws included — actual in the first place.
summary.takeaway: Appeals to the laws of nature cannot replace the simple cause, because the parts plus the law form a further composite, and on the Aristotelian view laws presuppose the form–matter composition they would be invoked to explain.
summary.deepDive:
This is the objection a scientifically educated skeptic is most likely to raise, so it is worth understanding thoroughly.

Take a worked example. Why does a water molecule hold together? Physics answers: the electromagnetic interaction binds the electrons and nuclei of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in a particular configuration. That answer is true, and Feser has no quarrel with it. The question is whether it *ends* the regress.

Look at what the explanation invokes: particles with specific charges and masses, and a law with a specific mathematical form and specific constants. Now ask: why are these particles governed by *this* law rather than some other one? Why do the constants have *these* values? The particles-plus-law package is itself a combination of distinct elements — things of certain types, and a law linking them. It is a new composite whose unity needs explaining. So the regress continues, just one level down. That is Feser's central point.

It helps to consider what a law of nature could be (chapter 7 surveys the options). If a law is just a description of a regularity, it explains nothing: it restates what happens. If it is a Platonic entity floating above the world, we need to explain why the world participates in *it* rather than another. If it is, as Aristotelians hold, shorthand for how things behave given their natures, then laws depend on the natures of the things themselves.

That last option is the subject of Feser's footnote, and it is subtle. One might think the Aristotelian view helps the critic, since laws are then internal to things rather than external rulers. It doesn't. A thing's nature, its substantial form, is one of the two basic principles it is composed of, along with prime matter. So a law's operating at all presupposes that form and matter are united. The law cannot be what explains that union; it is downstream of it.

Notice the overall shape: whatever the critic offers — a further part, a brute fact, a law — either restarts the regress or abandons explanation. Only something with no composition at all can end it (**steps 3, 6–8**). The usual confusion is to treat laws as agents that *do* things, as though ‘the law of gravity’ pulled objects around. Laws describe how things act; they are not additional things doing the acting.

checks.q: Why does Feser say that A, B, and the law governing them form ‘a kind of composite’?
options: Because we must still explain why A and B are governed by that law rather than another, so their being so governed is one more union needing a cause
Because laws are made of atoms
Because laws change over time
Because A and B are abstract objects
checks.explanation: The law-based explanation yields a further complex rather than something simple, so the regress continues.

checks.q: On the Aristotelian view in Feser's footnote, why can't a law explain a thing's composition?
options: Because Aristotelians deny that laws exist
A law describes how a thing acts given its substantial form, and form is one of the two principles, with prime matter, whose union needs explaining
Because laws are external rulers imposed by God
Because substantial forms are absolutely simple
checks.explanation: The operation of a law presupposes the form–matter composition, so it can't be what explains it.

checks.q: A physicist explains the stability of water by electromagnetic laws. By the chapter's lights, this explanation is…
options: false, because science cannot explain composition
a complete answer that ends the regress
true as far as it goes, but it leaves a further composite (particles plus laws with specific values) whose actual existence still needs explaining
irrelevant, because water is simple
checks.explanation: Feser does not dispute physics; he denies that a law-based explanation can terminate the regress.

argument.name: The Neo-Platonic Proof (the argument from composition)
argument.overview:
The argument has two stages.

**Stage 1 (steps 1–9)** runs from the fact that ordinary things are composite to the existence, here and now, of an absolutely simple cause. It rests on three claims: a composite exists at each moment only because its parts are combined at that moment (step 2); that combination needs a cause operating at the same time (step 3); and the resulting series of causes is hierarchical, so it must have a first member, which only something without parts could be (steps 7–8).

**Stage 2 (steps 10–38)** derives the attributes of this simple cause, mostly by one repeated move: *if it had X, it would have parts; it has no parts; so it lacks X.* That move yields uniqueness (10–13), immutability (14–15), beginninglessness and endlessness (16–17), eternity (18–19), uncausedness (20–21), and pure actuality (33–34). A separate argument by elimination, borrowed from Vallicella, shows that it is a mind (22–29). Uniqueness plus Stage 1 shows that it causes everything else (30–32). A link to chapter 1 adds perfection, omnipotence, goodness, and omniscience (35). The last steps gather the results and identify this cause with God (36–38).

> The engine of Stage 2 is a single idea: every distinction within a thing — between bearer and feature, actual and potential, what it is and that it is, before and after — is a kind of composition. Remove all composition and you remove every limitation.

stages.title: Stage 1 — From composites to an absolutely simple cause
stages.gist: Composites exist only while their parts are held together by concurrent causes; the hierarchical series of such causes must end in something with no parts at all.

stages.title: Stage 2a — Uniqueness
stages.gist: Two simple causes could only differ by a feature one has and the other lacks, which would make them composite; so there is exactly one.

stages.title: Stage 2b — Immutability, eternity, uncausedness
stages.gist: Change, beginning, ending, and being caused all require parts; the simple cause has none, so it is changeless, eternal, and uncaused.

stages.title: Stage 2c — Intellect
stages.gist: The simple cause is not abstract, material, or a mental content, so by elimination it is a mind.

stages.title: Stage 2d — Universal cause, pure act, and the classical attributes
stages.gist: Being unique, it causes everything else; lacking parts, it has no potency and is purely actual, hence perfect, omnipotent, good, and omniscient.

stages.title: Conclusion — This is God
stages.gist: A cause with all these attributes is what is meant by God, so God exists.

steps.text: Everything we experience is composite, made up of parts of some kind.
steps.why: Plain observation: chairs, books, and organisms all have parts, and scientific and metaphysical analysis reveals further parts (molecules and atoms; form and matter; essence and existence). The premise needs only that ordinary things have *some* kind of parts.
steps.example: A chair (legs, screws, seat), a tree (roots, trunk, leaves — and, for Aristotelians, form and matter), and you yourself (organs, cells, molecules) are all made of parts.
steps.challenge: Perhaps the most fundamental constituents of reality have no parts at all.
steps.answer: Step 1 concerns the things of our experience, which plainly have parts; and even a ‘fundamental’ particle has a definite nature distinct from its existence and potentials distinct from its actual state, so it is composite in the broad sense the chapter uses.

steps.text: At any moment a composite exists, it exists only because its parts are combined at that moment.
steps.why: A chair whose pieces lie in a heap, or are bolted together as a table, is no chair. This dependence is atemporal: it holds whether the thing was assembled, grew organically, came into being all at once, or even always existed.
steps.example: Pile the chair's pieces in the corner, or bolt them together as a table, and the chair no longer exists, though every piece still does.
steps.challenge: Once a thing has been put together, doesn't it simply go on existing by itself?
steps.answer: Feser's point is that a composite's existing at each moment consists in its parts being united at that moment; a chair that had always existed would be in the same position, so continued existence is not a default needing no ground.

steps.text: The combining of those parts requires a cause operating at the same time (a concurrent cause).
steps.why: The composite cannot cause its own composition without an explanatory vicious circle, since its existence depends on the combination. In fact we find outside factors doing the work at each moment: screws, friction, molecular and atomic bonds, a suitable temperature.
steps.example: At this moment, screws hold the legs to the frame, friction holds the screws, molecular bonds hold the wood, and a cool enough room keeps the metal from melting and the wood from burning.
steps.challenge: Why couldn't the composite itself be what keeps its parts together?
steps.answer: Its existence presupposes the union of its parts, so making it the cause of that union would be an explanatory vicious circle — the chair lifting itself by its own metaphysical bootstraps.

steps.text: So every composite has a cause of its existence at each moment it exists.
steps.why: From 2 and 3: if existing requires the parts to be combined, and the combining requires a concurrent cause, then existing requires a concurrent cause.
steps.example: Because the chair exists only while its parts are united, and that union needs a present cause, the chair has a present cause of its existence.

steps.text: So each of the things we experience has a cause at each moment it exists.
steps.why: Apply 4 to the composite things identified in 1.
steps.example: Your coffee cup, your dog, and you yourself each have, right now, causes of your continuing to exist.

steps.text: If the cause of a composite's existence at a given moment is itself composite, it will in turn need a cause of its own existence at that moment.
steps.why: This is simply step 4 applied to the cause: whatever made the first composite need a concurrent cause applies to any composite cause as well.
steps.example: The screws that hold the chair together are made of metal whose atoms must be bonded right now, so they too need present causes of their existence.
steps.challenge: Couldn't a composite cause be the kind of composite that needs no further cause?
steps.answer: No: step 4 applies to every composite for the same reason, and there is no principled basis for requiring a cause of the chair's composition while exempting the composition of its causes.

steps.text: The regress this generates is hierarchical, and a hierarchical regress must have a first member.
steps.why: Each member contributes only derived, borrowed causal power, like the stick that moves the stone only because the hand moves it. Without a first member whose power is not borrowed, nothing would be held in being at all (the argument of chapter 1). The members act simultaneously, but what makes the series hierarchical is the derivation, not the simultaneity.
steps.example: Atoms hold molecules together, molecules hold the wood together, the wood holds up the chair — each only because it is itself being held together, like the stick that moves the stone only because the hand moves it.
steps.challenge: Why not an infinite hierarchy of composite causes, each sustained by the next?
steps.answer: In a hierarchical series every member's causal power is derived, so an infinite series of borrowers explains no more than a finite one; without a member whose power is not borrowed there would be no causal activity at all (chapter 1).

steps.text: Only something absolutely simple, with no parts of any kind, could be the first member of such a series.
steps.why: Any composite member would itself need a cause of its composition (steps 4 and 6) and so would not be first. The first member must lack physical parts and metaphysical parts (form and matter, essence and existence) alike.
steps.example: If the proposed first member were an immaterial spirit whose essence differs from its existence, its essence and existence would themselves need uniting, so it could not be first.
steps.challenge: Couldn't the first member be composite but somehow self-sufficient?
steps.answer: A composite exists only while its parts are united and cannot cause that union itself (steps 2–3), so any composite depends on something further and is not first; the first must lack parts of every kind.

steps.text: So the existence of each thing we experience presupposes an absolutely simple cause.
steps.why: From 5–8: each composite has a concurrent cause; the series of such causes is hierarchical and must terminate; only a simple cause could terminate it. Following Plotinus, this cause is called the One.
steps.example: Right now, the chair's existence presupposes a simple cause at the bottom of the hierarchy of factors holding it together.
steps.challenge: Why think every composite's series ends in the same kind of thing?
steps.answer: Each such series must terminate (step 7) and only something simple could terminate one (step 8); whether there is one simple cause or many is settled in steps 10–13.

steps.text: For there to be more than one absolutely simple cause, each would need some distinguishing feature the others lacked.
steps.why: Two things are two only if something is true of one that is not true of the other. Without any differentiating feature they would be indistinguishable — not two things but one.
steps.example: Two steel balls from the same factory, however alike, still differ at least in their location and in the particular bits of steel they are made of.
steps.challenge: Couldn't two things differ merely numerically, without any distinguishing feature?
steps.answer: For material things, merely numerical difference is grounded in distinct matter or location; a simple being has neither, so there would be nothing to ground a second one's being second.

steps.text: But for a cause to have such a distinguishing feature would be for it to have parts, so it would not really be simple.
steps.why: A would be ‘simple cause plus F’ and B ‘simple cause plus G’: each would combine what it shares with the other and what sets it apart, which is a composition.
steps.example: If simple cause A had feature F that B lacked, A would be ‘simple cause plus F’ — a combination of what it shares with B and what sets it apart.
steps.challenge: Couldn't a distinguishing feature be something other than a part?
steps.answer: In the broad sense the argument uses, anything a thing has that another of its kind lacks is an element added to what they share, and so a constituent — exactly what simplicity excludes.

steps.text: So no absolutely simple cause can have a distinguishing feature.
steps.why: From 11: having such a feature is incompatible with simplicity.
steps.example: Just as a thing cannot be partless and have legs, it cannot be partless and have a feature that sets it apart from another of its kind.

steps.text: So there cannot be more than one absolutely simple cause.
steps.why: From 10 and 12: plurality requires differentiation, and simplicity rules differentiation out. The One is ‘one’ in the sense of unique as well as partless.
steps.example: The ultimate source of the chair's existence and the ultimate source of the stars' existence are one and the same simple cause.

steps.text: If the simple cause could change, it would have parts that it gains or loses — but being simple, it has no parts.
steps.why: To change is to gain or lose some feature, and a thing that can gain or lose a feature is the thing plus that feature — a composite.
steps.example: A person who learns Greek gains a new feature, and a leaf that turns red loses its green — each is ‘the thing plus a feature’ that can come or go.
steps.challenge: Couldn't the One change in some way that involves no gain or loss?
steps.answer: Change just is a thing's coming to be different; if nothing whatever is gained or lost, nothing has changed.

steps.text: So the simple cause is changeless (immutable).
steps.why: From 14 together with its simplicity (9).
steps.example: Unlike the leaf that changes color, the One has no feature it could acquire or shed.

steps.text: If the simple cause had a beginning or an end, it would have parts that could be put together or come apart.
steps.why: To begin to exist is to be caused, which means having one's parts combined; to cease to exist is to be broken down into parts.
steps.example: A chair begins when its parts are assembled and ends when they are broken apart; the One has no parts for either to happen to.
steps.challenge: Couldn't something simple just come into being, or be annihilated, without any parts being combined or separated?
steps.answer: To come into being is to be caused, and what is caused has parts needing combination (step 20); and Feser argues that being able to pass away implies having parts one could be broken down into — besides, a being that depends on nothing has nothing on which its existence hangs.

steps.text: So, since it has no such parts, the simple cause has neither beginning nor end.
steps.why: From 16 together with its simplicity.
steps.example: There was never a time before the One existed and there will never be a time after it.

steps.text: Whatever is changeless and without beginning or end is eternal.
steps.why: Being in time involves change; what cannot change, and neither starts nor stops, is not in time at all — it is eternal in the strict sense of being outside time.
steps.example: A star that burned forever would be everlasting but still in time, because it keeps changing; eternity in the strict sense means having no ‘before and after’ at all.
steps.challenge: Couldn't something be changeless yet still exist through time, like a rock sitting unchanged?
steps.answer: A rock only seems unchanging: it has potentials, weathers, and exists through successive moments as a changeable thing. What is strictly immutable has no succession in it to measure, and so is not in time.

steps.text: So the simple cause is eternal.
steps.why: From 15, 17, and 18.
steps.example: The One does not last through time; it exists outside time altogether.

steps.text: Whatever is caused has parts that need to be combined.
steps.why: On this argument's analysis, to cause something's existence just is to account for the union of its parts (pieces, form with matter, essence with existence). Where there is nothing to unite, there is nothing for a cause to do.
steps.example: When a sculptor causes a statue, he brings bronze and shape together; when a new animal is conceived, matter comes to be informed by a new substantial form.
steps.challenge: Can't a cause simply produce a thing from nothing, without combining parts?
steps.answer: Even what is produced from nothing is, if it is not God, a composite of essence and existence and of act and potency, so causing it is causing that union; a simple being offers nothing for a cause to unite.

steps.text: So the simple cause, having no parts, is uncaused.
steps.why: From 20. This is not an arbitrary exemption from a general rule: something absolutely simple not only needs no cause but could not have one.
steps.example: Asking what caused the One is like asking what glued together something that has no pieces.
steps.challenge: Isn't exempting God from causation just special pleading?
steps.answer: No: the principle is that composites need causes, so the simple is not an exception to the rule but outside its scope — and Feser notes this was the Neo-Platonic tradition's view from the start, not a later dodge.

steps.text: Everything is either a mind, a content of a mind, a material thing, or an abstract thing.
steps.why: Vallicella's classification of the basic kinds of entity, which Feser adopts.
steps.example: A mind (you), a mental content (your thought of a unicorn), a physical entity (a stone), and an abstract entity (the number seven).
steps.challenge: Why think these four categories are exhaustive?
steps.answer: Feser adopts Vallicella's classification and draws a hedged conclusion — a mind, or more like a mind than anything else; any fifth candidate would still have to be causally active, partless, and ultimate, which points the same way.

steps.text: Abstract things are causally inert.
steps.why: A stone can break a window, but the abstract pattern of being-a-stone cannot break anything or do anything at all.
steps.example: A stone can break a window; the abstract pattern of being-a-stone cannot break a window or do anything else.
steps.challenge: Don't abstract mathematical laws ‘govern’ physical events?
steps.answer: Mathematical structures describe how concrete things behave; the causing is done by the concrete things themselves. Taken by itself, an abstraction does nothing.

steps.text: So the simple cause, which is not causally inert, is not an abstract thing.
steps.why: From 23 and the fact that it causes the existence of composite things (9).
steps.example: The number seven, triangularity, or a pattern cannot be what holds the chair's atoms together right now.

steps.text: A material thing has parts and is changeable.
steps.why: Material things are made of parts that must be combined, and for that reason they can come into being and pass away.
steps.example: Any physical object, from a table to a galaxy, is made of parts and can be broken down or destroyed.
steps.challenge: What about a fundamental field or particle with no smaller parts?
steps.answer: It still has a nature distinct from its existence and states it could change into, so it remains composite and changeable in the broad sense the argument uses.

steps.text: So the simple cause, being partless and changeless, is not a material thing.
steps.why: From 25 together with 9 and 15.
steps.example: The One cannot be some subtle kind of matter or energy, since any such thing would have parts and be subject to change.

steps.text: A mental content presupposes a mind that has it, and so cannot be the ultimate cause of anything.
steps.why: A thought exists only as some mind's thought; the mind is prior to it, so the thought cannot be the ultimate source.
steps.example: Your idea of a unicorn exists only because you are thinking it; the thought depends on you, not you on it.
steps.challenge: Couldn't there be a thought with no thinker — a free-floating idea?
steps.answer: A mental content is by definition the content of some mind; a ‘thought’ belonging to no mind would really be an abstract entity, which is causally inert (step 23).

steps.text: So the simple cause, being the ultimate cause of things, is not a mental content.
steps.why: From 27 and 9.
steps.example: The ultimate cause of things cannot be anyone's idea, since that idea would depend on the mind that has it.

steps.text: So the simple cause must be a mind.
steps.why: By elimination from 22, 24, 26, and 28. Vallicella's hedge: it is a mind, or at least more like a mind than anything else. (Plotinus put intellect second, after the One; Feser departs from him here.)
steps.example: Having ruled out the stone, the number, and the thought, what remains is the category to which the thinker belongs.
steps.challenge: Isn't every mind complex — many thoughts, and a distinction between the thinker and what is thought?
steps.answer: Human minds are; but ‘mind’ applies to the One analogically, and classical theists such as Aquinas hold that in God knower, knowing, and known are one. Plotinus, by contrast, put intellect second for exactly this reason, which is where Feser departs from him.

steps.text: Since the simple cause is unique, everything other than it is composite.
steps.why: From 13: whatever is not the one simple cause cannot be simple, so it has parts.
steps.example: The chair, the stars, angels (if there are any), and the laws of physics are all composite, because only one thing is not.
steps.challenge: Couldn't there be other simple things that are not causes?
steps.answer: The differentiation argument of steps 10–13 applies to any two simple things: nothing could distinguish them, so there cannot be more than one simple being of any sort.

steps.text: Every composite has the simple cause as its ultimate cause.
steps.why: From Stage 1 (4–9) together with uniqueness (13): the hierarchical series behind every composite ends in a simple cause, and there is only one.
steps.example: Trace what holds your hand together right now, level by level, and you reach the very same simple cause as for the Andromeda galaxy.
steps.challenge: Couldn't different composites trace back to different ultimate causes?
steps.answer: Only if there were more than one simple cause, which steps 10–13 rule out.

steps.text: So the simple cause is the ultimate cause of everything other than itself.
steps.why: From 30 and 31.
steps.example: Nothing exists apart from the One except what depends on it for its existence.

steps.text: If the simple cause had potentialities as well as actualities, it would have parts.
steps.why: It must be at least partly actual, since the merely potential can do nothing and it causes everything. But a mixture of actuality and potentiality would be a composite of an actual ‘part’ and a potential ‘part’.
steps.example: Water is actually liquid and potentially ice: what it is now and what it could become are two distinct aspects of it — a kind of composition.
steps.challenge: Why must the One be actual at all — couldn't it be pure potential?
steps.answer: What is merely potential can't do anything (chapter 1), but the One is causing the existence of everything else; and a mix of actual and potential would make it composite, so it must be purely actual.

steps.text: So, since it has no parts, it has no potentialities and is purely actual.
steps.why: From 33 together with its simplicity.
steps.example: There is nothing the One could become that it is not already.

steps.text: A purely actual cause must be perfect, omnipotent, fully good, and omniscient.
steps.why: Carried over from chapter 1, using the principle of proportionate causality and the analysis of perfection and goodness as actuality. And since there can be only one purely actual being, the One is identical with the Unmoved Mover.
steps.example: A teacher can pass on a knowledge of algebra only if she has it in some way; likewise, whatever perfections are found in effects must be present in some way in their purely actual cause.
steps.challenge: Doesn't this simply import chapter 1's conclusions without argument?
steps.answer: It imports arguments already given in chapter 1 (and developed in chapter 6): pure actuality entails lacking all privation and being the source of all power, goodness, and intelligence. Since the One is purely actual, those arguments apply to it.

steps.text: So there exists a cause that is simple, unique, immutable, eternal, immaterial, a mind, the uncaused ultimate cause of everything other than itself, purely actual, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, and omniscient.
steps.why: Gathers the results of 9, 13, 15, 19, 21, 26, 29, 32, 34, and 35.
steps.example: The attributes derived one by one — simple, unique, immutable, eternal, immaterial, intelligent, uncaused, all-causing, purely actual, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, omniscient — belong to one and the same cause.
steps.challenge: Doesn't attributing so many features to one being contradict its simplicity?
steps.answer: No: the descriptions differ in sense but share one reference (like the morning and evening star), and they are predicated analogically; in the One they are one reality described in different ways.

steps.text: For such a cause to exist just is for God to exist.
steps.why: This list of attributes is what classical theism — the mainstream philosophical tradition and the Jewish, Christian, and Muslim traditions — means by ‘God’.
steps.example: Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, and Aquinas would each recognize this list as a description of God.
steps.challenge: Isn't this just a ‘philosopher's God,’ not the God of religion?
steps.answer: The attributes listed — unique, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, cause of all things — are exactly what the major monotheistic traditions ascribe to God; Feser says the first several alone already justify the name ‘God’.

steps.text: So God exists.
steps.why: From 36 and 37.
steps.example: The same being reached from change in chapter 1 is here reached from composition.

keyTerms.definition: Anything made up of parts of any kind, whose existence depends on those parts existing and being united in the right way. Word forms: ‘composite’ (noun or adjective), ‘composition’ (being made of parts), ‘compose’.
keyTerms.example: A chair (legs, screws, seat); a tree (form and matter); a particular triangle (essence and existence).
keyTerms.origin: Latin compositus, ‘put together’ (com- ‘together’ + ponere ‘to place’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Complicated’ — a composite need not be intricate (a lump of copper is still form plus matter); the word is about having parts, not about complexity.

keyTerms.definition: Any constituent or factor whose combination with others is required for a thing's existence — not only physical pieces but underlying constituents, sustaining conditions, and metaphysical principles.
keyTerms.example: Chair legs; the atoms in the wood; the room's temperature; a thing's form; its act of existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin pars; the scholastic tradition distinguishes integral (physical) parts from metaphysical principles.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical piece — a ‘part’ here includes principles like form or existence that cannot be separated or pointed to.

keyTerms.definition: Having no parts of any kind: no physical parts, no form/matter, no essence/existence, no actuality/potentiality, and no distinction between a bearer and its features. Word forms: ‘simple’, ‘simplicity’, ‘noncomposite’, ‘partless’.
keyTerms.example: Only the One qualifies. An immaterial angel still has an essence distinct from its existence, so it is not absolutely simple.
keyTerms.origin: Latin simplex, ‘onefold’ (literally ‘without folds’), as opposed to compositus.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Simple’ meaning easy or primitive — divine simplicity means partlessness, and the One is extremely hard to comprehend.

keyTerms.definition: Plotinus's name for the utterly simple first principle of all things; Feser's name for the simple cause reached by this argument.
keyTerms.example: It is ‘one’ in two senses: it has no parts, and there can be only one of it.
keyTerms.origin: Greek to hen; Plotinus's term, drawing on Plato's Parmenides and the Form of the Good in the Republic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Monism's ‘everything is one thing’ — the One is distinct from the composite things it causes, not identical with them.

keyTerms.definition: Greek-speaking philosopher (c. 204/5–270 AD), taught in Rome, founder of Neo-Platonism; his treatises were collected by his student Porphyry as the Enneads.
keyTerms.example: He ranked reality as the One, then Intellect, then Soul, with everything flowing from the One.
keyTerms.origin: Greek-speaking philosopher of the Roman Empire; his works were edited by his student Porphyry.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Plato — Plotinus, writing six centuries later, systematized Plato's ideas into the One–Intellect–Soul hierarchy.

keyTerms.definition: The tradition stemming from Plotinus that reads Plato's philosophy as a hierarchy of reality flowing from an utterly simple One; it deeply shaped Augustine, Pseudo-Dionysius, Islamic philosophy, and Aquinas.
keyTerms.example: Its guiding intuition: every multiplicity presupposes a prior unity.
keyTerms.origin: A modern historians' label (Greek neos, ‘new’ + Plato); its adherents simply called themselves Platonists.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Platonism in general — Neo-Platonism is the later school from Plotinus that places an utterly simple One above even the Forms.

keyTerms.definition: Dependence that holds at each moment regardless of history: what a thing needs right now in order to exist right now.
keyTerms.example: Even a chair that had always existed would need its legs attached and its molecules bonded at every moment.
keyTerms.origin: Greek a- ‘not’ + Latin tempus ‘time’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being eternal — atemporal dependence concerns things in time that depend on something at each moment; it does not make them timeless.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that operates at the same time as its effect, sustaining it rather than merely starting it. Also called a sustaining cause.
keyTerms.example: Friction keeping the screws in the chair while the chair exists.
keyTerms.origin: Latin concurrere, ‘to run together’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Originating cause — a concurrent cause sustains an effect while it exists; an originating cause only starts it off.

keyTerms.definition: A supposed explanation in which A depends on B while B depends on A, so neither is actually accounted for. Feser's image for it is ‘metaphysical bootstrapping’.
keyTerms.example: The chair's existence depends on its parts being united, so the chair cannot be what unites them.
keyTerms.origin: Latin circulus vitiosus, ‘faulty circle’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mutual support among pieces of evidence — here the circle concerns existence, and it explains nothing because each item's being hangs on the other.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member's causal power is derived from a prior member, so the whole series depends here and now on a first member with underived power. Also called an ‘essentially ordered’ series.
keyTerms.example: Hand–stick–stone; atoms holding molecules holding legs holding up the chair.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per se, ‘through itself’: the series is ordered essentially, each member acting only through the one prior.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simultaneous series — simultaneity is typical, but what defines a per se series is derived causal power.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which earlier members need not still exist or act for later members to act. Also called an ‘accidentally ordered’ series.
keyTerms.example: The factory worker who assembled the chair years ago; he can die and the chair remains.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per accidens, ‘incidentally’: the members are related only incidentally.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Any series in time — what matters is that earlier members need not still act, not simply that they came earlier.

keyTerms.definition: In Aristotelian metaphysics, the principle that makes a thing the kind of thing it is and gives it its characteristic properties; universal, the same in every member of a kind.
keyTerms.example: Copper's form gives malleability and electrical conductivity; a tree's form gives the power to draw nutrients through roots.
keyTerms.origin: Greek eidos or morphē; Latin forma. Part of Aristotle's hylomorphism (hylē ‘matter’ + morphē ‘form’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Shape — shape is one changeable feature; form is what makes a thing the kind of thing it is.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that ties a universal form down to a particular individual here and now; on its own it is mere potentiality to be something.
keyTerms.example: What makes this piece of copper a different individual from that piece, though both have the same form.
keyTerms.origin: Greek hylē (originally ‘timber’); Latin materia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Matter in the modern physical sense (atoms, mass) — Aristotelian prime matter is pure potentiality, not already-formed stuff.

keyTerms.definition: What a thing is; its nature.
keyTerms.example: The essence of triangle: a closed plane figure with three straight sides.
keyTerms.origin: Latin essentia, from esse ‘to be’; the scholastic rendering of Aristotle's ‘what it is to be’ a thing.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Existence — essence is what a thing is; existence is that it is.

keyTerms.definition: The fact that a thing is; its actual being, distinct in each individual. Word forms: ‘exist’, ‘existence’, and the Latin ‘esse’.
keyTerms.example: The existence of this triangle on the whiteboard, as distinct from that one's.
keyTerms.origin: Latin exsistere, ‘to stand forth’; Aquinas's esse, the ‘act of being’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence — knowing what a triangle is tells you nothing about whether any particular triangle exists.

keyTerms.definition: Something one thing has and another lacks, by virtue of which they are two rather than one; possible only for composites.
keyTerms.example: If simple cause A had F and simple cause B had G, each would be ‘simple cause plus a feature’ — composite.
keyTerms.origin: Related to the scholastic differentia, the specific difference that divides a genus into species.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A merely verbal difference — any real feature one has and another lacks counts, even location or relation.

keyTerms.definition: Changelessness: the inability to gain or lose any feature. Word forms: ‘immutable’, ‘immutability’, ‘changeless’.
keyTerms.example: The One cannot change, since what can gain or lose a feature is composed of itself plus that feature.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- ‘not’ + mutabilis ‘changeable’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness — the One is changeless because it is fully actual, not because it is inactive; it causes everything.

keyTerms.definition: Existing outside time (because changeless) and without beginning or end. Word forms: ‘eternal’, ‘eternity’, ‘timeless’.
keyTerms.example: Not ‘lasting a very long time’, which would still be temporal, but being altogether outside time.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas; Boethius's classic definition is the complete, simultaneous possession of unending life.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness — lasting through endless time is still temporal; eternity in the strict sense is being outside time.

keyTerms.definition: An entity such as a number, pattern, or universal considered in itself, neither physical nor mental; causally inert. Word forms: ‘abstract’, ‘abstraction’, ‘causally inert’; the opposite is ‘concrete’ (an actual individual thing).
keyTerms.example: The pattern of being-a-stone cannot break a window; only an actual stone can.
keyTerms.origin: Latin abstrahere, ‘to draw away’: considered apart from concrete things.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Immaterial thing — a mind is immaterial but not abstract; abstract things are causally inert, minds are not.

keyTerms.definition: Something that exists only as the product or object of a mind, such as a thought.
keyTerms.example: Your idea of a triangle exists only because you are thinking it.
keyTerms.origin: One of the four categories in William Vallicella's classification, adopted by Feser.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mind — the mind is the thinker; a mental content, such as a thought, depends on the thinker.

keyTerms.definition: Being wholly actual with no unrealized potential; chapter 1's description of the Unmoved Mover. Word forms: ‘purely actual’, ‘pure act’ (Latin actus purus).
keyTerms.example: The One must be purely actual, since a mix of actual and potential would be a composite.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus; from Aristotle's energeia, ‘being-at-work’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Maximal busyness — pure act means no unrealized potential, not ceaseless motion.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in some way present in its total cause; a cause cannot give what it does not in some way have.
keyTerms.example: Used (via chapter 1) to show that a purely actual cause has intellect, power, and goodness.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic principle; Feser abbreviates it PPC and defends it at length in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Principle of causality (PC) — PC says that what is actualized (or composite) needs a cause; PPC says what that cause must possess.

keyTerms.definition: Frege's distinction between the way an expression presents its object (sense) and the object it picks out (reference).
keyTerms.example: ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ differ in sense but both refer to Venus.
keyTerms.origin: Gottlob Frege, ‘On Sense and Reference’ (1892); German Sinn and Bedeutung.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Synonymy — two expressions can share a reference without having the same meaning.

keyTerms.definition: Using a term in exactly the same sense in two contexts. Word forms: ‘univocal’, ‘univocally’.
keyTerms.example: ‘Rover is a dog’ and ‘Fido is a dog’.
keyTerms.origin: Latin univocus, ‘one-voiced’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication — univocal keeps an identical sense; analogical keeps a related but different one.

keyTerms.definition: Using a term in two completely unrelated senses. Word forms: ‘equivocal’, ‘equivocally’, ‘equivocation’.
keyTerms.example: A baseball bat and the bat flying around the attic.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aequivocus, ‘equally voiced’: one word, unrelated meanings.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication — equivocal senses are unrelated; analogical senses are related.

keyTerms.definition: Using a term in senses that are neither identical nor unrelated; still literal, not metaphorical. Aquinas's account of how we speak of God. Word forms: ‘analogy’, ‘analogical’, ‘analogically’; ‘predication’ means saying something of a subject.
keyTerms.example: ‘The wine is good’ and ‘George is a good man’.
keyTerms.origin: Greek analogia, ‘proportion’; developed systematically by Thomas Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphorical predication — metaphor is non-literal; analogical predication is literal.

keyTerms.definition: A fact that has no explanation at all.
keyTerms.example: The critic's suggestion that the union of a thing's parts is simply unexplained.
keyTerms.origin: Term from contemporary analytic philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unknown explanation — a brute fact has no explanation at all, not merely one we have not yet found.

keyTerms.definition: The classical doctrine that God has no parts of any kind, so that his attributes are really identical with one another and with his essence and existence. Word forms: ‘divine simplicity’, ‘God is simple’.
keyTerms.example: God's power, knowledge, and goodness are one reality described in different ways (developed in chapter 6).
keyTerms.origin: Core of classical theism, affirmed by Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, and Avicenna; taught by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and the First Vatican Council.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theological simplism — divine simplicity is a precise metaphysical thesis about partlessness, not a claim that God is easy to understand.

keyTerms.definition: Shorthand for how a thing tends to act given its substantial form; so it presupposes the thing's composition of form and matter rather than explaining it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Copper conducts electricity’ describes what copper's form disposes it to do.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Thomist tradition; Feser returns to the nature of laws in chapter 7.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A law as an external decree — on this view laws describe how natures act rather than being rules imposed from outside.

keyTerms.definition: The form that makes a thing the fundamental kind of substance it is (copper, tree, dog), as opposed to accidental forms such as shape or color.
keyTerms.example: What makes an oak an oak rather than a heap of cellulose; if it is lost, the oak ceases to exist.
keyTerms.origin: Latin forma substantialis; Aristotle and the scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Accidental form — color or shape can change while the substance remains; a change of substantial form means the thing itself is gone.

keyTerms.definition: Matter considered as pure potentiality, with no form at all; it never exists on its own, only as informed by some form.
keyTerms.example: What underlies the change when wood burns to ash: not an actual thing, but the capacity to take on new forms.
keyTerms.origin: Latin materia prima; Aristotelian-Thomist metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Elementary particles — particles are already formed things; prime matter is formless potential.

keyTerms.definition: Distinct principles that together make up a concrete thing but cannot exist separately: form and matter, essence and existence, actuality and potentiality, a bearer and its features.
keyTerms.example: You cannot pull a tree's form out of its matter, yet they are really distinct principles of the tree.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic metaphysics; Feser uses the phrase in contrast to ordinary physical parts.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Integral (physical) parts — those can be separated or pointed to; metaphysical parts cannot.

keyTerms.definition: The physical, quantitative parts of a whole, which can in principle be separated from one another.
keyTerms.example: The legs, screws, seat, and cushion of a chair.
keyTerms.origin: Latin partes integrales, ‘parts that make up a whole’; scholastic usage.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical parts — integral parts are pieces; metaphysical parts are principles.

keyTerms.definition: The way a thing really is at a given moment, as opposed to the ways it merely could be. Word forms: ‘actual’, ‘actuality’, ‘act’, ‘actualize’ (to make actual).
keyTerms.example: A cup of coffee's actually being hot.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus; Greek energeia or entelecheia (Aristotle).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Activity — actuality means being real in some respect, not necessarily doing something.

keyTerms.definition: A thing's real capacity to be or become otherwise; on its own it can do nothing. Word forms: ‘potential’, ‘potentiality’, ‘potency’.
keyTerms.example: The coffee's potential to become cool, which the surrounding air actualizes.
keyTerms.origin: Latin potentia; Greek dynamis (Aristotle).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere logical possibility — a potency is a real capacity rooted in a thing, not just something that isn't contradictory.

keyTerms.definition: Chapter 1's conclusion: the purely actual cause that actualizes potentials without itself being actualized. Chapter 2 shows it is identical with the One.
keyTerms.example: The first member of the hierarchy that sustains the coffee's existence right now.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Metaphysics Book XII; Latin primum movens immobile.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The first domino in a temporal chain — ‘first’ means ultimate and underived, not earliest.

keyTerms.definition: Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. This chapter's counterpart is that whatever is composite has a cause of its composition.
keyTerms.example: The chair's parts are united now only because screws, friction, and bonds are uniting them now.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic principle defended by Feser in chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Everything has a cause’ — PC applies only to what is actualized or composite, which is why God is not covered by it.

keyTerms.definition: Everything has an explanation, either in itself or in something else.
keyTerms.example: The reason Feser can dismiss ‘maybe there's no explanation’ as unserious is closely related to the PSR.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with Leibniz; defended by Feser in chapter 5 (the Rationalist proof).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality — the PSR concerns explanation of anything whatsoever; PC concerns causes of actualization or composition.

keyTerms.definition: A series with no first member, each item depending on a further one without end. Word forms: ‘regress’, ‘regression’.
keyTerms.example: Unifying parts A and B with a further part C, then C with D, then D with E, forever.
keyTerms.origin: Latin regressus, ‘going back’; regressus in infinitum.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A benign infinite series — a linear series might in principle be infinite; the problem is a hierarchical one, where every member's power is borrowed.

keyTerms.definition: A cause whose causal power is not derived from anything else — first in the order of dependence, not necessarily in time.
keyTerms.example: The hand, relative to the stick and the stone; the One, relative to every composite.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa prima.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The earliest cause in time — the argument's ‘first’ member operates here and now.

keyTerms.definition: In Plotinus, the second level of reality after the One: divine mind eternally thinking the Forms. Feser, unlike Plotinus, attributes intellect to the One itself. Word forms: ‘intellect’, ‘intellectual’, ‘mind’.
keyTerms.example: Plotinus put intellect second because thinking seemed to involve a duality of thinker and thought.
keyTerms.origin: Greek nous, ‘mind’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The One — for Plotinus, Intellect comes after the One and involves a kind of duality.

keyTerms.definition: The third level of Plotinus's hierarchy, below Intellect, which animates and orders the physical cosmos.
keyTerms.example: The World-Soul giving life and order to the heavens and to living things.
keyTerms.origin: Greek psychē.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The individual human soul — Plotinus's Soul is a cosmic principle, of which individual souls are expressions.

keyTerms.definition: The collection of Plotinus's fifty-four treatises, arranged by his student Porphyry into six groups of nine.
keyTerms.example: Plotinus's discussion of unity as the condition of being appears in the sixth group (Ennead VI).
keyTerms.origin: Greek ennea, ‘nine’.

keyTerms.definition: Plotinus's picture of how all things flow from the One, like light from the sun, without diminishing their source. Feser's argument neither needs nor defends this detail.
keyTerms.example: Intellect proceeding from the One, and Soul from Intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Latin emanare, ‘to flow out’; Greek proodos, ‘going forth’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Creation by free choice — later theists (Augustine, Aquinas) held that God creates freely, not by necessary overflow.

keyTerms.definition: What can be present in many things at once — for Aristotelians, a form shared by every member of a kind.
keyTerms.example: The one form of copper present in this lump, that lump, and a third.
keyTerms.origin: Latin universalis, ‘pertaining to all’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A particular — a particular is this individual; the universal is what many individuals share.

keyTerms.definition: What makes a thing this particular individual rather than another of the same kind; for Aristotelians, matter. Word forms: ‘individuate’, ‘individual’.
keyTerms.example: Two copper coins of identical form are two because they are made of different parcels of matter.
keyTerms.origin: Latin individuare, ‘to make indivisible/single’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Differentiation by kind — individuation distinguishes members of one kind; specific difference distinguishes kinds.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term non-literally, on the basis of some resemblance. Word forms: ‘metaphor’, ‘metaphorical’, ‘metaphorically’.
keyTerms.example: ‘God is my rock’ — God is not literally a rock, but is steadfast like one.
keyTerms.origin: Greek metaphora, ‘carrying over’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication — ‘God is good’ is literal and analogical; ‘God is a rock’ is metaphorical.

keyTerms.definition: The mainstream conception of God in Western philosophy and the Abrahamic religions: simple, immutable, eternal, purely actual, the ground of all being.
keyTerms.example: The God of Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, and Aquinas, whom all five proofs aim to reach.
keyTerms.origin: Label used by modern philosophers of religion for the tradition from Plato and Aristotle through the scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism — which treats God as a very great person with distinct properties, often denying simplicity.

keyTerms.definition: A modern view (discussed in chapter 6) that treats God as the greatest member of the category ‘person’, with distinct attributes, and often denies divine simplicity.
keyTerms.example: Alvin Plantinga's criticism of simplicity, which Feser answers in chapter 6.
keyTerms.origin: Label applied by Brian Davies; also called ‘neo-theism’ by Norman Geisler.
