keyTerms.confuseWith: Believing that God is personal — classical theists also hold that God has intellect and will; the difference is over simplicity.

keyTerms.definition: Arbitrarily exempting one case from a general rule without a principled reason.
keyTerms.example: ‘Everything has a cause — except God, because I say so.’
keyTerms.origin: Traditional name for an informal fallacy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled restriction — the composition principle applies only to composites by its very content, so exempting the simple is not arbitrary.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming, in an argument, the very thing that is in dispute.
keyTerms.example: Rejecting the simple cause merely because one assumes in advance that no such being exists.
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, ‘assuming the starting point’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Raising the question’ — in everyday speech the phrase is often misused this way.

keyTerms.definition: The finding of quantum physics that elementary particles show both particle-like and wave-like properties.
keyTerms.example: Feser's example of a conclusion that is hard to understand yet well supported, because it concerns things far from everyday experience.
keyTerms.origin: Early twentieth-century physics (Einstein, de Broglie, Bohr).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Incoherence — being hard to picture is not the same as being contradictory.

keyTerms.definition: Having all power: being able to actualize any potential that can coherently be actualized. Word forms: ‘omnipotent’, ‘omnipotence’, ‘all-powerful’.
keyTerms.example: As the source of all actualizing power, the purely actual cause has all possible power (chapter 1).
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis ‘all’ + potens ‘powerful’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being able to do the logically impossible — omnipotence concerns all that is possible.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing everything that can be known. Word forms: ‘omniscient’, ‘omniscience’, ‘all-knowing’.
keyTerms.example: Derived from the One's being purely actual and an intellect, with the principle of proportionate causality.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis ‘all’ + scientia ‘knowledge’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Merely having very extensive information — omniscience is complete, not just vast.

keyTerms.definition: Being complete, lacking nothing a thing of its kind should have; in God, the absence of any unrealized potential or privation. Word forms: ‘perfect’, ‘perfection’.
keyTerms.example: A purely actual being is perfect because it has no unactualized potential.
keyTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, ‘thoroughly made, completed’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral flawlessness only — metaphysical perfection concerns completeness of being, of which moral goodness is one aspect.

keyTerms.definition: Being without matter; not a physical thing. Word forms: ‘immaterial’, ‘immateriality’, ‘incorporeal’.
keyTerms.example: The One is immaterial because material things have parts and can come to be and pass away.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- ‘not’ + materia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Absolute simplicity — an immaterial creature like an angel still has an essence distinct from its existence.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that everything is either a mind, a mental content, a physical entity, or an abstract entity; used to show by elimination that the One is a mind.
keyTerms.example: Ruling out abstract (inert), physical (composite), and mental-content (dependent) options leaves mind.
keyTerms.origin: William F. Vallicella, A Paradigm Theory of Existence (2002).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Descartes's mind–body dualism — Vallicella's scheme has four categories, and adds mental contents and abstracta.

keyTerms.definition: In Plotinus, one of the three fundamental levels of reality — the One, Intellect, and Soul — each deriving from the one above it. (In later Christian theology the word came to mean ‘person’.)
keyTerms.example: Intellect is the second hypostasis, proceeding from the One; Soul is the third.
keyTerms.origin: Greek hypostasis, ‘that which stands under’: a foundation or underlying reality.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Substance in Aristotle's sense — a hypostasis is a level of reality in the Neo-Platonic hierarchy, not an individual thing like a dog.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God is identical with the universe or with everything in it. A close relative is monism, the view that all reality is ultimately a single thing.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 7 notes that if the universe itself were uncaused and necessary, the result would be pantheism rather than atheism — but the universe is composite.
keyTerms.origin: Greek pan ‘all’ + theos ‘god’; the word was coined in the early 1700s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism — the One is distinct from the composite world it causes; everything other than it is composite, and it is not.

keyTerms.definition: An argument, developed by medieval Islamic thinkers and defended today by William Lane Craig, that the universe began to exist and therefore has a cause. Unlike Feser's proofs, it depends on the universe's having a beginning.
keyTerms.example: A critic who assumes every cosmological argument is about the Big Bang is thinking of the kalām version.
keyTerms.origin: Arabic kalām, ‘speech’: the name of medieval Islamic dialectical theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Neo-Platonic proof — which concerns what sustains things here and now and is indifferent to whether the universe began.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle's theory that every physical substance is a composite of form and matter. Word forms: ‘hylomorphism’, ‘hylomorphic’.
keyTerms.example: On hylomorphism, a tree is matter organized by the substantial form of a tree; when the tree dies, the same matter comes under other forms.
keyTerms.origin: Greek hylē ‘matter’ + morphē ‘form’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mind–body dualism — hylomorphism concerns every physical thing, and its form and matter are two principles of one thing, not two separate things.

keyTerms.definition: Word forms: ‘contingent’, ‘contingency’. A contingent thing is one that could have failed to exist; its essence does not guarantee its existence.
keyTerms.example: You, your dog, and the laws of physics are contingent; chapter 7 uses this to show that none of them could be the uncaused cause.
keyTerms.origin: Latin contingere, ‘to happen, to befall’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Accidental’ in the everyday sense of unplanned — a contingent thing need not be random; it simply does not exist by necessity.

keyTerms.definition: Having no cause of one's existence. In this chapter only the absolutely simple is uncaused, because only composites need, or could have, a cause; ‘uncaused cause’ names such a being.
keyTerms.example: Step 21: the simple cause, having no parts, is uncaused.
keyTerms.origin: Traditional phrase, parallel to Aristotle's ‘unmoved mover’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Self-caused — something uncaused has no cause at all, whereas a self-caused thing would be its own cause, which Feser calls incoherent.

keyTerms.definition: Being the only one of its kind, with no possible rival. The classical name for this divine attribute is ‘unity’. Word forms: ‘unique’, ‘uniqueness’.
keyTerms.example: Steps 10–13 prove the uniqueness of the simple cause.
keyTerms.origin: Latin unicus, ‘only, sole’; unitas, ‘oneness’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplicity — simplicity is having no parts; uniqueness is there being only one. The One has both, and the second follows from the first.

keyTerms.definition: On the Aristotelian analysis, a thing is good to the extent that it actualizes the potentials proper to its kind; the purely actual cause, lacking no actuality, is fully good. Word forms: ‘good’, ‘goodness’.
keyTerms.example: A good painter is one who fully realizes a painter's skills; God, lacking nothing, is goodness without limit.
keyTerms.origin: Chapter 1's analysis, drawing on Aristotle and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere moral niceness — goodness here is completeness of being, of which moral goodness is one form.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God cannot be fully understood by any finite mind, though we can know truly that he exists, what he is not, and something of what he is by analogy. Word forms: ‘incomprehensible’, ‘incomprehensibility’.
keyTerms.example: Feser: reason itself shows there is a level of reality that reason can only partly comprehend.
keyTerms.origin: Latin incomprehensibilis, ‘not able to be grasped completely’; developed in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Unknowability — incomprehensible means not fully graspable, not totally unknowable.

keyTerms.definition: An argument meant to establish its conclusion with necessity, by strict deduction from premises that are themselves certain, rather than to make it probable or ‘the best explanation’.
keyTerms.example: Feser (chapter 7) says his five proofs are demonstrations, not quasi-scientific hypotheses that some alternative might in principle beat.
keyTerms.origin: Latin demonstratio; Aristotle's apodeixis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A scientific hypothesis — a hypothesis is the best available explanation, open to revision; a demonstration claims deductive necessity.

keyTerms.definition: The interpretation of quantum mechanics on which some physical events (such as when a radioactive atom decays) are not fixed in advance by prior conditions.
keyTerms.example: Some critics, such as Victor Stenger, claim quantum events happen without causes; Feser replies (chapter 1) that lacking a deterministic cause is not lacking a cause.
keyTerms.origin: Twentieth-century physics, notably the Copenhagen interpretation.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Acausality — an indeterministic event is not strictly predictable, but it still occurs within a system with conditions and causal structure.

keyTerms.definition: Invented just for the case at hand, to escape a difficulty, rather than following from an independent principle.
keyTerms.example: Critics call the restriction of the causal principle to composites an ad hoc dodge; Feser replies that the tradition held it from the start and that it follows from what composition is.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad hoc, ‘for this (purpose)’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ad hominem — ad hoc describes a claim patched on for convenience; ad hominem attacks the person rather than the claim.

keyTerms.definition: Rejecting a claim because of something about the person making it, such as their motives, rather than on its merits.
keyTerms.example: ‘Theists only say God is uncaused because they want to dodge the question’ — even if true of someone's motives, that wouldn't show the claim false.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad hominem, ‘to the person’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ad hoc — see that entry.

keyTerms.definition: The regress, named after F. H. Bradley, that arises when a relation is treated as one more item that must itself be related to its terms; a close cousin of the reply to the ‘further part’ objection.
keyTerms.example: If glue relates two boards, what relates the glue to each board? And what relates that?
keyTerms.origin: F. H. Bradley, Appearance and Reality (1893). The comparison with Feser's argument is the course's, not Feser's.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Any infinite series — the problem is not length but that each proposed unifier itself needs unifying.

keyTerms.definition: A twentieth-century school (Charles Hartshorne and others) holding that God changes and develops along with the world; a form of theistic personalism that denies divine immutability.
keyTerms.example: By the chapter's reasoning, a changing God would gain and lose features and so be composite and caused.
keyTerms.origin: Inspired by Alfred North Whitehead's ‘process philosophy’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism — which holds that God is immutable because simple.

keyTerms.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies parts and wholes. Its ‘special composition question’ asks when several things together make up a further thing.
keyTerms.example: Mereological universalists say any things whatever compose a further object; mereological nihilists say there are no composite objects, only simples ‘arranged chair-wise’.
keyTerms.origin: Greek meros, ‘part’; term coined by the logician Stanisław Leśniewski.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Neo-Platonic question — mereology asks when composition occurs; the Neo-Platonic argument asks what makes a composite's parts actually exist and be united.

keyTerms.definition: A feature a substance can gain or lose while remaining the same kind of thing, such as shape, color, or temperature.
keyTerms.example: Copper hammered into a bowl changes its accidental form (shape) but keeps its substantial form (it is still copper).
keyTerms.origin: Latin forma accidentalis; from Aristotle's category of ‘accidents’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Substantial form — losing an accidental form changes a thing; losing its substantial form destroys it.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of something a thing ought to have, given its nature; a lack, not merely a non-presence.
keyTerms.example: Blindness in a dog is a privation; a stone's lack of sight is not.
keyTerms.origin: Latin privatio, ‘deprivation’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere absence — a stone lacks sight without being deprived of it.

keyTerms.definition: A genus is a broad kind (animal); a specific difference is what marks off one species within it (rational, for humans). Chapter 6 argues God falls under no genus, since that would make him composite.
keyTerms.example: ‘Human = rational animal’: animal is the genus, rational the specific difference.
keyTerms.origin: Latin genus ‘kind’ and differentia specifica; from Aristotle's logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Differentiating feature — any feature that distinguishes two things; a specific difference distinguishes species within a genus.

keyTerms.definition: God's continual sustaining of creatures in existence at every moment, as opposed to merely starting them off; the here-and-now dependence this proof relies on.
keyTerms.example: Just as the chair needs its parts united right now, everything depends right now on God in order to exist.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conservatio, ‘keeping, preserving’; treated in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Creation at a first moment — conservation concerns continued existence, whether or not there was a first moment.

keyTerms.definition: An individual thing that exists in its own right, like a dog, a tree, or a lump of copper, as opposed to features that exist only in something else, like color or shape.
keyTerms.example: ‘Every physical substance is a composite of form and matter.’
keyTerms.origin: Latin substantia, ‘what stands under’; Aristotle's ousia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Substance’ in the everyday sense of a material, as in ‘a sticky substance’.

keyTerms.definition: The hypothesis that our universe is one of many universes.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 7: a multiverse could not be the uncaused cause, because it is composite.
keyTerms.origin: Term from modern cosmology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The universe — even many universes together would be one more (larger) composite.

keyTerms.definition: The philosophical tradition following Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), which develops Aristotle's metaphysics and adds, among other things, the real distinction between essence and existence. Word forms: ‘Thomism’, ‘Thomist’, ‘Thomistic’.
keyTerms.example: Thomist philosophers distinguish what a triangle is from the fact that a given triangle exists.
keyTerms.origin: From the name of Thomas Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelianism — Thomism builds on Aristotle but adds distinctively Thomistic doctrines such as the essence–existence distinction.

keyTerms.definition: The tradition following Aristotle (384–322 BC), whose central tools include actuality and potentiality and form and matter. Word forms: ‘Aristotelian’, ‘Aristotelianism’.
keyTerms.example: The Aristotelian proof of chapter 1 reasons from change (the actualizing of potentials) to a purely actual cause.
keyTerms.origin: From the name of Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Platonism — Plato placed the Forms in a separate realm, whereas Aristotle holds that forms exist in things.

keyTerms.definition: The medieval and later tradition of systematic philosophy and theology taught in the universities, whose most famous representative is Aquinas. Word forms: ‘scholastic’, ‘Scholasticism’.
keyTerms.example: Feser's book Scholastic Metaphysics defends the scholastic analysis of form and matter and of essence and existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin scholasticus, ‘belonging to the school’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Pedantry — in everyday speech ‘scholastic’ can mean hair-splitting; here it names a tradition.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that acts only by virtue of power it receives from a prior cause, like a tool in a hand; the members of a hierarchical series after the first are instrumental.
keyTerms.example: The stick moving the stone is an instrumental cause; the hand is the principal cause.
keyTerms.origin: Latin causa instrumentalis; scholastic usage.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Linear (per accidens) cause — instruments belong to hierarchical series, where their power must be continually supplied.

keyTerms.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies the most general features of reality: being, causation, change, parts and wholes, essence and existence. Word forms: ‘metaphysics’, ‘metaphysical’.
keyTerms.example: The claim that composites need a cause of their composition is metaphysical, not a finding of a particular science.
keyTerms.origin: Greek meta ta physika, ‘after the physics’ — the title given to Aristotle's treatise placed after his Physics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The occult or ‘New Age’ sense of the word, which has nothing to do with the philosophical discipline.

distinctions.name: Two senses of ‘more fundamental’

left.label: Whole prior to parts (for understanding)
left.desc: We understand a part by its role in the whole: a leg is for moving about, an eye for seeing, a book cover for protecting the pages, a cushion for comfort.

right.label: Parts prior to whole (for existence)
right.desc: The whole cannot exist unless its parts exist and are arranged the right way; heap them up, scatter them, or build a table instead and the chair is gone.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument runs on the second sense. Seeing both keeps you from caricaturing it as treating wholes as mere heaps; it grants the whole's priority for understanding while noting that the whole's being depends on its parts' union.

distinctions.name: Temporal vs. atemporal dependence

left.label: Temporal (historical)
left.desc: The parts existed first and were later assembled, as with a manufactured chair. True of some composites but not all — a body's organs develop together.

right.label: Atemporal (moment by moment)
right.desc: At every moment it exists, a composite needs its parts united at that moment — whether it was assembled, grew, appeared all at once, or always existed.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Because the argument uses atemporal dependence, it is untouched by debates over whether the universe had a beginning, and it concludes to a cause operating now rather than merely long ago.

distinctions.name: Linear vs. hierarchical causes of a composite

left.label: Linear (per accidens)
left.desc: The worker who assembled the chair; he can retire or die and the chair stays put. For all this argument cares, such a series could stretch back forever.

right.label: Hierarchical (per se)
right.desc: Screws, friction, molecular and atomic bonds, suitable temperature: each contributes only what it derives from deeper factors, and all must be at work for the chair to exist now.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only a hierarchical series must have a first member. That is what forces the regress to end in something with underived existence — which must then be partless.

distinctions.name: Physical vs. metaphysical parts

left.label: Physical (integral) parts
left.desc: Pieces you could in principle point to or separate: legs, screws, pages, organs, molecules, atoms.

right.label: Metaphysical parts (principles)
right.desc: Distinct but inseparable principles that together make up a concrete thing: form and matter, essence and existence, actuality and potentiality, a bearer and its features.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The One must lack both. Something with no physical parts (a soul, an angel) could still be metaphysically composite and so still need a cause. Absolute simplicity is far stronger than mere immateriality.

distinctions.name: ‘Everything has a cause’ vs. ‘Whatever is composite has a cause’

left.label: What critics attack
left.desc: An exceptionless principle that everything whatsoever has a cause — which would indeed demand a cause for God.

right.label: What the argument says
right.desc: Only what has parts needs a cause of their union; what is absolutely simple neither needs nor could have one.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This dissolves ‘What caused God?’. God is not a special-pleading exception; the principle simply does not apply to what has no parts, much as ‘all triangles have three sides’ says nothing about circles.

distinctions.name: Sense vs. reference

left.label: Sense
left.desc: The way an expression presents its object; its meaning. ‘The One is omnipotent’ and ‘the One is an intellect’ differ in sense.

right.label: Reference
right.desc: The object an expression picks out. ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ both pick out Venus.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It shows how many true, non-synonymous descriptions of God (powerful, intelligent, eternal) can all be about one simple reality without introducing parts into it.

distinctions.name: Univocal vs. analogical predication (with equivocal as the other extreme)

left.label: Univocal
left.desc: Same sense in both uses: ‘dog’ said of Rover and of Fido. (At the opposite extreme, equivocal use has wholly unrelated senses: ‘bat’ for the club and the animal.)

right.label: Analogical
right.desc: Related but not identical senses: ‘good’ said of wine and of George. Still literal, not metaphorical.

distinctions.whyItMatters: If ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ applied to God exactly as they do to us, they would name distinct features — parts. Used analogically, they say there is something in God corresponding to each, while in him they are one.

distinctions.name: An alternative explanation vs. no explanation

left.label: Alternative explanation
left.desc: A rival account of why the parts are united (a further part? the laws of nature?), which must then be assessed on its merits — and each such account regenerates the problem.

right.label: No explanation (brute fact)
right.desc: Simply declaring that the union of the parts has no explanation at all.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Critics often present ‘it's just a brute fact’ as though it competed with the Neo-Platonic explanation. It doesn't; it declines to explain. With an explanation on the table and no non-question-begging reason to reject it, ‘maybe there's no explanation’ is not a serious reply.

illustrations.title: The chair you are sitting on
illustrations.body:
Feser's central example. Your chair has legs, screws, a frame, a seat, a cushion. Pile those pieces in the corner, or bolt them together as a small table, and you no longer have a chair: the chair needs its parts to exist *and* to be arranged a certain way.

Now ask what keeps them arranged right now. Screws hold the legs to the frame; friction keeps the screws in place; the wood and metal hold together because their molecules are bonded, and the molecules because their atoms are. Even the room's temperature is doing work: make it hot enough and the screws melt and the wood burns. At every moment the chair exists, a whole stack of factors must be combined just so. The chair contributes none of this to itself.

illustrations.title: The body that was never assembled, and the chair that always existed
illustrations.body: One might think ‘dependence on parts’ just means ‘was put together at some time’. Feser blocks this with two cases. Your body was never assembled from ready-made arms and eyes; the organs all developed together as cells divided in the womb. And imagine a chair that had existed forever, or one that popped into being all at once. In every case the thing still depends, at each moment, on its parts existing and being united at that moment. The dependence the argument cares about is about *now*, not about the past.

illustrations.title: Copper, trees, and animals: one form, many things
illustrations.body: Why are three separate lumps all copper rather than lead or gold? For the Aristotelian, because they share one and the same form, which gives them malleability and conductivity. Likewise every tree shares the form of tree (drawing up water through roots) and every animal the form of animal (sensing through organs). What makes this lump a different copper *thing* from that one is its matter. But the form apart from matter is only an abstraction, and matter apart from form is only a potential to be something. Neither can supply the union of the two, so even at this deep metaphysical level the thing needs a cause of its composition.

illustrations.title: The triangle: what it is and that it is
illustrations.body: The essence of triangle — a closed plane figure with three straight sides — is shared by every triangle, while each triangle has its own existence. You never meet a triangle's existence without its being a triangle; and the essence on its own, belonging to no actual triangle, is just an abstraction. So in any concrete triangle, essence and existence lean on each other, and something outside the triangle must account for their being joined. Feser uses this to show that the composition principle applies even to parts no microscope could reveal.

illustrations.title: The glue that needs glue
illustrations.body: Feser, following Vallicella, considers the suggestion that one part of a thing unites the others. Picture two boards, A and B, joined by glue, C. What joins the glue to the boards, and holds the glue itself together? Posit a further binder D, and you must ask what joins D to A, B, and C. Each new ‘unifier’ is just another part that needs unifying. Adding parts never explains unity; it only lengthens the list of things to be unified.

illustrations.title: The morning star and the evening star
illustrations.body: Ancient observers named a bright light in the dawn sky and a bright light in the evening sky as if they were two things. ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ really do mean different things — each phrase presents its object differently — but both refer to one planet, Venus. Feser uses Frege's example to show that ‘the One's power’ and ‘the One's intellect’ can differ in meaning while referring to one simple reality. Many descriptions do not entail many parts.

illustrations.title: Good wine and a good man
illustrations.body: Call a dog ‘a dog’ and another dog ‘a dog’ and you use the word the same way (univocally). Call a club a ‘bat’ and a flying mammal a ‘bat’ and the meanings have nothing to do with each other (equivocally). But say the wine is good and George is good, and the meanings are neither identical nor unrelated: the wine's goodness and George's goodness are analogous. No metaphor is involved; both are literally good. This is how, following Aquinas, we should speak of God's goodness, power, and intellect.

illustrations.title: Wave–particle duality
illustrations.body: Physics tells us that electrons and photons behave in some ways like particles and in some ways like waves. Nobody can picture that well, yet the evidence and theory compel it — and we should *expect* difficulty, because we are stretching concepts built for tables and pebbles to cover things far beyond everyday experience. Feser argues that the ground of all reality is farther still from everyday experience, so it would be suspicious if our concepts did *not* strain when applied to it. Difficulty of comprehension is a predicted feature of the conclusion, not evidence against it.

illustrations.title: The army and the chorus (Plotinus)
illustrations.body: Plotinus liked to point out that an army, a chorus, or a flock exists as such only while it has unity. Disband the army and the soldiers still exist, but the army is gone; scatter the singers and there is no chorus. The same holds for a house or a living body. His conclusion: being and unity go together, every many presupposes a one, and so the source of all things must be unity itself. Feser's chair argument is a modern, step-by-step version of this ancient insight.

illustrations.title: The magnetic sculpture
illustrations.body:
Imagine a sculpture of loose steel pieces that stays standing only because an electromagnet in its base is switched on. Nothing in the sculpture holds the sculpture together; cut the current and it collapses at once — even if it had stood there forever. The magnet in turn works only because current flows from a generator, which runs only because something else drives it. Each level holds only because something deeper holds it.

Use this to show: (1) atemporal dependence (the sculpture's unity must be sustained now); (2) the further-part mistake (pointing to one steel piece as ‘the holder’ just adds a piece that also needs holding); (3) the hierarchy (borrowed holding-power at every level). And mark where the analogy breaks: the One is not one more physical power source at the bottom of the stack, but the partless ground on which every level, including the laws of electromagnetism, depends.

objections.title: “Even if there's a first cause, why call it God?”
objections.whoRaises: Popular skeptics; a common reaction to any cosmological argument
objections.objection: Grant, for argument's sake, that composite things trace back to something simple. That is a far cry from God. The ultimate cause might be an impersonal force, a physical field, or something we have no name for. Jumping from ‘first cause’ to the God of theism is wishful thinking.
objections.reply:
Feser answers that this objection is lazy in the context of this argument, because Stage 2 gives specific reasons for each divine attribute.

- It must be **unique**, because two simple things could differ only by a feature one has and the other lacks — which would make them composite.
- It must be **changeless and eternal**, because change, beginning, and ending all require parts.
- It is **not physical**, because physical things have parts; **not abstract**, because abstractions cause nothing; **not a mental content**, because thoughts depend on minds. So it is a **mind**.
- It must be **purely actual**, since a mix of act and potency is a composition; and from pure actuality chapter 1 derives perfection, omnipotence, goodness, and omniscience.

One may criticize any of those steps (and chapter 6 takes up such criticisms), but one cannot simply assert that the cause need not be divine.
objections.pushback: If the objector says ‘an impersonal field could be simple,’ ask whether a field has parts or structure, varies from place to place, has values it could lack, or could have been otherwise. Any of these makes it composite. If they say ‘fine, but maybe your attribute arguments fail,’ agree that this is the right place for the debate — and ask which specific step they reject.

objections.title: “The argument assumes the universe had a beginning”
objections.whoRaises: Critics familiar with the kalām argument; anyone who hears ‘first cause’ as ‘earliest cause’
objections.objection: Arguments like this depend on tracing causes back to a first moment. But modern cosmology leaves open that the universe (or a multiverse) is past-eternal. If there was no first moment, there is no first cause.
objections.reply: The argument makes no claim about a first moment. Its dependence is **atemporal**: at any moment a composite exists, it needs its parts united at that moment. Feser explicitly says that even an everlasting chair would depend on its parts. The regress is not traced backward in time to a beginning but downward, here and now, to a cause that is sustaining things at this very moment. The word ‘first’ means ‘ultimate, underived’, not ‘earliest’. So the argument goes through whether the universe is past-eternal or not.
objections.pushback: If they insist that every causal argument is secretly about time, walk through the chair in a heated room: whether or not the chair has existed forever, it would fall apart *now* if the conditions sustaining it failed now. That's the kind of dependence at issue.

objections.title: “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”
objections.whoRaises: Bertrand Russell's lineage; Richard Dawkins and many popular writers
objections.objection: The argument says things need causes. Then God needs a cause too. If God can be uncaused, why not the universe? Either way, calling God the exception is special pleading.
objections.reply: The argument never says everything has a cause. Its premise is that **whatever is composite** needs a cause of its composition. God is not an arbitrary exception: something absolutely simple has nothing to be put together, so it not only needs no cause but *could not* have one. Nor is this a dodge invented to escape the objection; it was the point of the Neo-Platonic tradition from the start. And the universe cannot play God's role, because the universe is massively composite. Feser concludes that the objection, far from devastating, completely misses the target.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘you just defined God as uncaused,’ reply that simplicity was not stipulated; it was argued for (steps 6–8): any composite cause would need a further cause, so the regress can only end in something partless. The uncausedness then follows from the partlessness. If they say ‘then the universe could be simple,’ ask how something with galaxies, particles, and changing states could lack parts.

objections.title: Hume and quantum mechanics: things can exist without causes
objections.whoRaises: David Hume; appeals to quantum indeterminacy (e.g., Victor Stenger)
objections.objection: Hume showed we can conceive of something existing without a cause, so causal principles aren't necessary truths. And quantum mechanics shows that some events happen without causes. So why believe every composite needs a cause of its composition?
objections.reply:
Feser refers the reader back to his replies in chapter 1, which apply equally here. In brief:

- Imagining something appearing without *also imagining* its cause is not conceiving of it as having *no* cause — just as thinking of a trilateral without thinking ‘triangle’ doesn't show a trilateral could fail to be a triangle.
- Experience overwhelmingly supports causal principles: we find causes when we look, and things don't pop into being at random.
- Quantum indeterminism at most shows some events lack *deterministic* causes, not that they lack causes; quantum systems still have structure and conditions.

Applied to this chapter: even an electron in a quantum state is something whose features and constituents must actually be joined for it to exist. Indeterminacy about what it will do next doesn't show that its existence right now needs no ground.
objections.pushback: If they press that the principle is merely an empirical generalization that could fail, note that the composition premise is not a claim about sequences of events but about what it is to be a whole: a whole just is its parts-united, and a union of distinct items is not self-explanatory. Ask them to describe a case where a thing's parts are united without anything accounting for it — not merely without *us* knowing what does.

objections.title: Many attributes mean many parts
objections.whoRaises: Critics of divine simplicity; thoughtful students on first hearing
objections.objection: The argument ends by listing a dozen attributes: omnipotence, intellect, goodness, eternity, and so on. But having many distinct attributes is having many parts. So the conclusion contradicts the premise that the One is absolutely simple.
objections.reply: Feser's first answer uses Frege's **sense/reference** distinction. ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ differ in meaning but refer to one planet. Similarly, ‘the One is omnipotent’ and ‘the One is an intellect’ are not synonymous, yet both can refer to one simple reality. Different *concepts* of God are not different *components* in God. The attributes are one and the same reality, conceived or described in different ways because our finite minds must approach it from different angles.
objections.pushback: If they reply that Venus is still composite, agree: the example only shows that difference of meaning does not require difference of reality, not that Venus is simple. The simplicity comes from the argument; the Frege point merely removes the apparent contradiction.

objections.title: “But in us intellect and power really are different things”
objections.whoRaises: Sharper critics of divine simplicity (the kind of worry Alvin Plantinga develops, discussed in chapter 6)
objections.objection: Sense and reference doesn't help. In a human being, intelligence and strength aren't just two descriptions of one thing; they're genuinely distinct features — a genius can be weak, a strong man foolish. If God has intelligence and power, those are distinct features in God too.
objections.reply: Feser grants the premise about humans and concedes that the conclusion would follow *if* the terms applied to God in exactly the same sense. But precisely because the One has no parts, they should not be applied **univocally**. Following Aquinas, they are used **analogically**: not in the same sense as with us (univocal), nor in a wholly unrelated sense (equivocal, like ‘bat’), but in a related sense (like ‘good’ said of wine and of a man). To say God has power and intellect is to say there is in God something analogous to what we call power and intellect in ourselves. And one respect in which God's ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ differ from ours is exactly that in him they are one reality, whereas in us they are two. Analogical speech remains literal, not metaphorical.
objections.pushback: If the critic says analogy is a way of saying nothing, point out that we use analogical terms literally all the time (‘good’ wine, ‘good’ man; ‘healthy’ food, ‘healthy’ person) and understand them perfectly well. If they demand a full picture of how power and intellect can be identical, grant that we lack one — and turn to the next objection.

objections.title: Divine simplicity is incomprehensible, and so suspect
objections.objection: A being whose knowledge is identical to its power, which is identical to its goodness, is not something anyone can actually understand. When a conclusion is this strange, that's a sign something went wrong in the argument.
objections.reply: Feser admits the conclusion is odd, but says we should *expect* it to be. Physics offers a parallel: particles behave like both waves and particles, which no one can properly picture, yet we accept it because the evidence and reasoning demand it and because the domain is remote from everyday experience. Reasoning to the absolutely simple ground of all reality goes farther from everyday experience than physics ever does, so our concepts must stretch to their limit. It would be surprising if the result were *not* hard to grasp. Reason itself tells us there is a level of reality reason can only partly comprehend. Difficulty of comprehension is not the same as incoherence.
objections.pushback: If they say wave–particle duality is backed by experiment and this is not, reply that the analogy concerns the *expected difficulty* of concepts stretched to remote domains, not the kind of evidence. The evidence here is the argument itself; if it is sound, the strangeness must be accepted, and they should identify which premise fails.

objections.title: A further part could do the unifying
objections.whoRaises: Critics of the external-cause premise (discussed by Vallicella)
objections.objection: Why assume the cause of a thing's unity must lie outside it? Perhaps some part of the thing — a binding element, a structural principle — is what unites the other parts.
objections.reply: Following Vallicella, Feser argues that this merely relocates the problem. Suppose a thing has parts A and B, and we say part C unites them. Now we need to know what unites C with A and B. Positing a part D pushes the question back again, and so on for every new part. Instead of explaining A and B's unity, we have created more things whose unity needs explaining. A unifier that is itself one of the items to be unified cannot do the job.
objections.pushback: If the objector says C is special — a ‘relation’ rather than a thing — ask whether that relation is really distinct from A and B. If it is, the question ‘what joins the relation to its relata?’ arises again; if it isn't, then nothing has been added to explain the unity.

objections.title: The unity is just an irreducible fact about the thing
objections.whoRaises: Critics who resist the demand for explanation
objections.objection: Some facts are basic. Perhaps the fact that a thing's parts are united is simply an irreducible fact about that thing — no external cause required.
objections.reply:
Feser asks what ‘irreducible fact’ means here. Two readings are possible:

1. The composite itself causes its parts to be united. Then it would be both the cause and the effect of the same union — incoherent, a thing lifting itself by its own bootstraps.
2. The union has no cause at all; it's a brute fact. Then the critic has not given an alternative explanation, which is what he claimed to offer. He has given no explanation.

Either way, nothing has been offered that competes with the Neo-Platonic account.
objections.pushback: If they insist that brute facts are respectable in philosophy, note that this abandons the claim to have an *alternative* and moves to the next objection — the claim that maybe there is no explanation at all.

objections.title: “Maybe there's simply no explanation”
objections.whoRaises: Critics biting the bullet; defenders of brute facts
objections.objection: Fine — I have no alternative explanation. I'm simply suggesting that there may be no explanation at all of why composite things exist. That possibility is enough to block your argument.
objections.reply: As Lloyd Gerson points out, this is not a serious response to the Neo-Platonic argument. Its defender can reply: an explanation *has* been given — the parts are joined by an absolutely simple cause — and the critic has offered no reason to reject it that doesn't beg the question. Saying ‘maybe there's no explanation’ while one sits on the table is like a detective who, handed a well-supported solution, replies that perhaps the crime has no culprit. One needs a reason to reject the explanation, not merely the observation that one could refuse to explain.
objections.pushback: If they respond that the explanation is unfalsifiable or extravagant, ask what makes it so — and note that its only posit is the minimal thing any unity of parts requires: something that unites without itself needing to be united. (Chapter 5 defends the principle of sufficient reason more directly.)

objections.title: Science and the laws of nature explain composition
objections.objection: We know exactly why things hold together: electromagnetic forces bind atoms into molecules, the strong force binds quarks into protons, and so on. The laws of nature explain composition. No God required.
objections.reply:
Feser grants that such explanations are true as far as they go, but denies that they are an alternative to the argument's conclusion. Any explanation in terms of laws leaves us with a further composite. If it is a law that things of type A and type B combine under certain conditions, we must ask why A and B are governed by *that* law rather than another. A, B, and the law together form a new complex whose unity itself needs explaining — so the regress continues rather than ends.

On the Aristotelian view, laws aren't external rulers at all but summaries of how things behave given their substantial forms. That only makes things worse for the critic: substantial form is one of the two principles (with prime matter) the thing is composed of, so the working of a law presupposes the very composition it was meant to explain. However laws are construed, only something absolutely simple can end the regress.
objections.pushback: If they say the regress ends at the most fundamental law or field, ask whether that law or field has structure, several parameters, or a nature distinct from the fact that it obtains. It could have been otherwise, so it has an essence distinct from its existence. Physics describes *how* composition works at each level; the argument asks what makes the whole hierarchy of levels actual. (Chapters 7a and 7b return to laws of nature.)

objections.title: Why not stop at fundamental particles, a quantum field, or the universe itself?
objections.whoRaises: Modern naturalists; Dawkins, Krauss and others as cataloged in chapter 7 (course application)
objections.objection: Physics tells us there are fundamental particles with no smaller parts. Those are the simples. Or take the universe as a whole, or the quantum vacuum, as the ultimate uncaused reality. Why leap to God?
objections.reply: The argument's notion of a part is broader than ‘smaller physical piece.’ An electron has no smaller spatial parts, but it still has a determinate nature (mass, charge, spin) that is distinct from the fact that it exists; it has states it is in and states it could be in (actuality and potentiality); it could have failed to exist. By the chapter's own reasoning, that makes it metaphysically composite and in need of a cause. The universe is obviously composite, since it's made of all these things. A quantum field has structure, values varying across space, and a nature that could have been otherwise. Only something with no distinction whatsoever between what it is and that it is, or between what it is and what it could be, can end the regress. In chapter 7 Feser applies exactly this reasoning: the universe and a multiverse cannot be uncaused precisely because they are composite, and the laws of physics lack the required simplicity.
objections.pushback: If they deny that essence/existence or act/potency are real distinctions, recall that the argument doesn't need them for most things: physical and structural composition already rules out the universe and fields. Metaphysical parts are needed only to show that even ‘partless’ particles don't escape.

objections.title: The ‘mind’ step is a false trichotomy
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers skeptical of the attribute derivations (course application)
objections.objection: Steps 22–29 assume that everything is a mind, a mental content, a material thing, or an abstract thing. Why think that list is exhaustive? Perhaps the ultimate cause is a fifth kind of thing we cannot categorize. And minds, as we know them, are complex — how could something utterly simple think?
objections.reply: Feser flags the modesty of the conclusion: following Vallicella, the One is ‘either a mind, or more like a mind than anything else.’ So the elimination does not claim to picture a divine mind; it locates the One nearer to mind than to any other category we know. That fits the analogical account: divine intellect is not a human-style process with parts but something analogous to it. The inference is also reinforced by chapter 1's argument from proportionate causality, carried over in step 35: a cause must in some way possess what it produces, and intellect is among the things the One produces. Chapter 6 develops divine intellect at length. Note, too, that Plotinus himself denied intellect to the One — so this is a point where Feser consciously revises the tradition he borrows from.
objections.pushback: If they propose a mysterious fifth category, ask what it would be like: if it causes, it isn't inert like an abstraction; if it is partless, it isn't material; if it is ultimate, it isn't a dependent thought. Whatever it is, it must possess, in a higher way, whatever is found in its effects — including thought. That is all ‘more like a mind than anything else’ claims.

objections.title: A partless being would be empty — or an abstract property
objections.whoRaises: Alvin Plantinga and other theistic personalists (answered in chapter 6)
objections.objection: If God is identical to each of his attributes, then all his attributes are identical to one another, and God is just one property. But properties are abstract objects. So divine simplicity turns God into an abstract object — or, if he has no properties, into a featureless blank.
objections.reply: Feser answers Plantinga in chapter 6, but the key moves are already present in chapter 2. First, simplicity is not emptiness: the One is *purely actual*, the fullness of being with no unrealized potential, not a bare something with nothing to it. Second, the objection interprets ‘power’, ‘knowledge’ and ‘property’ univocally, as if God had them in the same way we do and as if properties were Platonic abstract objects. Classical theists reject both assumptions; attributes are predicated analogically, and God is never said to be a ‘property’ at all. Third, this chapter itself argues that the One cannot be an abstract entity, since abstractions are causally inert and the One is the cause of everything.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘then I don't understand what simplicity means,’ return to the positive content: no parts, no potentiality, no dependence. Everything we know about composite things tells us what God is *not*; the analogical terms tell us what in God corresponds, in a higher way, to perfections in creatures.

misconceptions.myth: The Neo-Platonic proof argues that the universe must have had a beginning.
misconceptions.correction: It is indifferent to whether the universe had a beginning. The dependence of a composite on its parts is atemporal, holding at each moment; the regress is traced down to a present sustaining cause, not back to a first moment.

misconceptions.myth: The argument rests on the premise that everything has a cause.
misconceptions.correction: Its premise is that whatever is composite has a cause of its composition. Something absolutely simple not only needs no cause but could not have one — so God is not a special-pleading exception.

misconceptions.myth: ‘Simple’ means primitive, empty, or easy to understand.
misconceptions.correction: It means partless. The One is the fullness of actuality with no parts, potentials, or limits — and Feser stresses that it is very hard to understand, as we should expect.

misconceptions.myth: Being immaterial is the same as being simple, so a soul or an angel could be the One.
misconceptions.correction: Absolute simplicity rules out metaphysical composition too (form/matter, essence/existence, act/potency, bearer/feature). An immaterial creature still has an essence distinct from its existence, so it is composite and caused.

misconceptions.myth: You must accept Aristotelian form and matter or Thomistic essence and existence for the argument to work.
misconceptions.correction: Feser says explicitly that nothing rides on those theories. The principle ‘whatever is composite has a cause’ is completely general and works with ordinary physical parts. The metaphysical parts simply show how far the principle reaches.

misconceptions.myth: Feser's proof is just Plotinus's system, so accepting it commits you to emanation and to intellect being below the One.
misconceptions.correction: Feser adopts the general Neo-Platonic strategy — from composition to an absolutely simple source — and departs from Plotinus by concluding that the One is itself a mind, as later thinkers like Augustine and Aquinas did.

misconceptions.myth: If God's attributes are spoken of analogically, then talk about God is merely metaphorical.
misconceptions.correction: Analogical predication is literal. Wine and George are both literally good, in related but different senses. God is literally powerful and wise, in a sense analogous to, not identical with, ours.

misconceptions.myth: The One and the Unmoved Mover are two different ultimate beings reached by two different proofs.
misconceptions.correction: Both are purely actual, and there can only be one purely actual being, so they are the same reality. The two proofs are different routes (parts/whole vs. act/potency) to the same summit.

misconceptions.myth: The regress must end simply because infinite chains are impossible.
misconceptions.correction: The point is the hierarchical character of the series: every member has only borrowed ‘holding-together’ power, so without an unborrowed source there would be none at all. A linear series (like a line of chair-makers) is not what the argument says must terminate.

misconceptions.myth: Feser claims the argument lets us fully comprehend God's nature.
misconceptions.correction: He says the opposite: reason shows there is a level of reality that reason can only partly comprehend, and the difficulty is exactly what we should expect (the wave–particle analogy).

misconceptions.myth: The conclusion is pantheism: the One is everything, or everything is the One.
misconceptions.correction: Everything other than the One is composite and the One is not, so it is distinct from the world it causes. Chapter 7 notes that treating the universe itself as uncaused would be pantheism, but the universe is composite and so cannot fill that role.

misconceptions.myth: If God is simple, he has no attributes, so we can say nothing true about him.
misconceptions.correction: Many true, non-synonymous statements can refer to one simple reality (sense vs. reference), and terms like ‘good’ and ‘wise’ apply literally, by analogy.

explain.tweet: Everything around us is made of parts, and parts don't hold themselves together. What holds them together right now? If that's made of parts too, ask again. The chain has to end in something with no parts at all: one, changeless, eternal, a mind, pure act. That's God.
explain.elevator: Pick anything — a chair, a cell, an atom. It exists only while its parts are held together, and it can't hold itself together, because its own existence depends on that union. So something else is doing it, right now. If that something has parts too, the question repeats, and each level only passes along borrowed holding-power. So the chain must end in something with no parts at all. And a thing with no parts turns out to be unique, changeless, eternal, a mind — God.
explain.twoMinute:
Here's an argument that goes back to the third-century philosopher Plotinus, in Edward Feser's modern version.

Start with anything around you — say the chair you're sitting on. It's made of parts: legs, screws, a seat. And it only exists as long as those parts are there *and* put together the right way. Pile the pieces in a corner and the chair is gone. That's true of everything we experience: tables, trees, bodies, molecules. They're all wholes made of parts.

Now, what holds the parts together? Not the chair itself — the chair only exists because the parts are already together, so it can't be what brings them together. That would be pulling itself up by its bootstraps. In fact other things are doing it: screws, friction, the bonds between molecules and atoms, even the room's temperature. Notice this isn't about the past. Even if the chair had existed forever, it would need all of that working *right now*.

But screws, molecules, and atoms are made of parts too, so they need something holding *them* together, now. And so on down. Every level has only borrowed holding-power, like a stick that moves a stone only because a hand is moving the stick. Unless there's something at the bottom that holds things together without needing to be held together itself, nothing would hold together at all. And the only thing that doesn't need holding together is something with no parts whatsoever — not even the subtle ‘parts’ philosophers talk about, like a thing's nature versus its existence.

Then the fun part: what would such a thing be like? There can only be one, because two would need some difference between them, and a difference is a part. It can't change, since changing means gaining or losing something. So it's outside time. It isn't physical, since physical things have parts; it isn't an abstraction, since abstractions don't cause anything. That leaves something like a mind. It has no unrealized potential, so it's pure actuality — the same thing Feser's first proof, from change, arrives at.

So the question ‘what caused God?’ misses the point. Only things with parts need causes. The argument isn't that everything has a cause; it's that everything with parts does, and that's why there has to be something without them.
explain.eli12:
Think of a Lego castle. It's only a castle while the bricks are clicked together. If you dump the bricks in a box, the castle is gone, even though every brick is still there.

Now, the castle can't be what clicks its own bricks together, because there's no castle until they're clicked! Something else has to do it. For a Lego castle, it's the little bumps and friction of the bricks. But those bricks are made of plastic, and plastic is made of tiny molecules that also have to be stuck together, and molecules are made of atoms, and atoms are made of even smaller bits. Everything that's made of pieces needs something else to keep its pieces together — right now, not just when it was built.

If *everything* was made of pieces, then every level would be waiting on the level below, forever, and nothing would actually be holding anything together. So there has to be something at the very bottom that isn't made of pieces at all. It doesn't need anyone to hold it together, because there's nothing in it to fall apart.

That something is very special. There can only be one of it (two would need to be different somehow, and being different means having something extra — a piece). It can't change, because changing means getting or losing a piece. It's not a thing you can touch. It's more like a mind than anything else. People have called it ‘the One’ — and it's what people mean by God.
whiteboard: Draw a simple chair. Label its parts: legs, screws, seat. Say: this chair exists only while these parts are united.
Next to it, draw the same parts in a heap. Write ‘parts, but no chair’. Point: a whole needs its parts AND their union.
Draw an arrow from the chair back to its own parts with a big X. Write ‘vicious circle’: the chair can't unite its own parts.
Below the chair, draw a vertical ladder: screws/friction → molecules → atoms → … Label it ‘right now’, not ‘in the past’. Write ‘hierarchical: borrowed holding-power’.
At the bottom of the ladder, draw a single dot with no parts. Label it ‘THE ONE: absolutely simple’. Say: only something with nothing to unite can end the ladder.
Draw a box listing kinds of parts: physical pieces | constituents and conditions | form + matter | essence + existence | act + potency. Say: the One lacks all of them.

Draw rays from the dot, one per attribute, each with ‘because no parts’: unique (no differentiating feature), changeless (nothing to gain or lose), eternal, uncaused, not material, not abstract, a mind, purely actual.
Draw a second road arriving at the same dot, labeled ‘Chapter 1: change → pure act (Unmoved Mover)’. Write ‘same summit’.
Write ‘Everything has a cause’ and strike it out. Replace with ‘Whatever is COMPOSITE has a cause’. Say: that's why ‘What caused God?’ misfires.
Write ‘morning star = evening star’ and ‘good wine / good man’. Say: many descriptions, one simple reality; analogical, not univocal.
explain.keyAnalogy:
**The magnetic sculpture.** Picture a sculpture of loose steel pieces that stands only because an electromagnet in its base is switched on. Nothing in the sculpture holds it together; cut the power and it collapses instantly, even if it had been standing forever. The magnet in turn works only because current flows from somewhere else, and so on down.

Use it in three moves. First, to show *atemporal* dependence: the question is not who built the sculpture but what holds it up *now*. Second, to expose the ‘further part’ reply: pointing to one steel piece as ‘the holder’ just adds another piece that needs holding. Third, to show the *hierarchy*: every level has only borrowed holding-power, so without an unborrowed source nothing would hold.

Then mark the limit of the analogy honestly: the One isn't one more power station at the bottom of a physical stack. It is the partless reality on which every level — including the laws of electromagnetism and the very existence of the steel — depends.

persuade.coreInsight:
The argument clicks when someone sees that **being united is not something parts get for free**. Most people unconsciously treat unity as the default: of course the chair holds together; that's what chairs do. It clicks when they notice that a whole is always a union of items that could have been apart or arranged differently, that this union is a real fact needing an explanation at every moment, and that the thing itself cannot supply that explanation without circularity. Once composition is seen as an ongoing *achievement* rather than a given, the question ‘what is achieving it right now, all the way down?’ becomes unavoidable — and ‘something that needs no uniting because it has nothing to unite’ becomes the natural answer.

The usual reasons it fails to click: people hear ‘cause’ as ‘past event’ and picture a builder who finished long ago; or they think of parts only as Lego-like pieces and assume that once physics reaches fundamental particles we have found the simples. Address both. Stress the moment-to-moment dependence (the chair in a room that could get hot enough to burn it). And widen the notion of part: even a particle has a nature distinct from the fact that it exists, and potentials distinct from what it actually is.

audiences.startingPoint: Believes physics already explains why things hold together (forces, fields, laws) and that talk of ‘metaphysical parts’ is armchair speculation.
audiences.approach: Agree enthusiastically that physics explains composition *at each level* — then show that every scientific explanation of a unity appeals to further unities: particles plus fields plus laws with specific values. Ask what makes that whole package actual right now. Lead with physical parts and structure; bring in essence/existence only when they propose a ‘fundamental’ entity as the stopping point. Use Feser's point that any law-based explanation yields a new composite (A, B, and the law) whose unity is exactly what needs explaining.
audiences.openingQuestion: When physics explains why two atoms bond, does it ever explain the bond by something that has no structure of its own?
audiences.avoid: Don't present the argument as competing with physics or as a ‘God of the gaps’ filling some region science hasn't reached. It's a question about the existence of the whole hierarchy physics describes.

audiences.who: Analytic philosophy student who knows mereology
audiences.startingPoint: Familiar with the ‘special composition question’; may hold that composition is automatic (any items compose a sum) or that strictly there are no composites, only simples arranged chair-wise.
audiences.approach: Clarify that the argument's ‘composition’ is not only about when sums exist but about what makes a thing's constituents *actually* exist and be united — including metaphysical constituents like essence and existence. If they say composition is ‘ontologically innocent’, ask what makes the parts themselves actual and so arranged. If they are nihilists about composites, move to the simples: do those particles have a nature distinct from their existence, and potentials distinct from their actual states? Then the argument applies to them.
audiences.openingQuestion: Suppose composition is automatic: does that explain why these particles exist and stand in these relations right now?
audiences.avoid: Don't get bogged down in debates over whether chairs ‘really’ exist. Feser's premise survives either answer, since the parts themselves are composite in the broader sense.

audiences.who: Believer who pictures God as a very great person among other beings
audiences.startingPoint: Believes in God but thinks of him as a supremely powerful, wise individual — one being alongside others, with distinct properties — and finds ‘divine simplicity’ cold or abstract.
audiences.approach: Show that simplicity is what makes God *God* rather than a super-creature. If God had parts, he would need a cause of their union, like everything else, and would not be ultimate. Use the chapter's logic: uniqueness, eternity, and uncausedness all come from simplicity. Then reassure them with the analogical point: God is literally good, wise, and powerful — just not in a way that divides him into pieces. Preview chapter 6's warning that a composite God would be a kind of superangel.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God were made of parts, what would hold those parts together?
audiences.avoid: Don't imply that simplicity makes God impersonal. The argument concludes to a mind, and Feser (unlike Plotinus) places intellect in the One itself.

audiences.who: Spiritual seeker drawn to ‘the One’ and non-dual traditions
audiences.startingPoint: Resonates with talk of an ultimate unity behind the many, perhaps from Advaita Vedanta, Buddhism, or Plotinus himself; may assume that the One is impersonal or that everything simply *is* the One.
audiences.approach: Start with the shared intuition Plotinus captured: every many presupposes a one. Then show the argument's precise refinements. The One is distinct from composite things (everything other than it is composite, and it is not), so the result is not pantheism. And it is mind-like, not an impersonal force, because it can't be abstract, material, or a mere thought. Present Feser's God as the fulfillment of their intuition rather than its rejection.
audiences.openingQuestion: If the ultimate reality is perfectly one, could it be identical with a world that is so obviously many?
audiences.avoid: Don't dismiss mystical traditions or use combative apologetic language. And don't overclaim that Plotinus agreed with Feser on everything; he didn't on intellect.

audiences.startingPoint: Has heard ‘What caused God?’ and ‘science explains everything’ and thinks cosmological arguments are about the Big Bang.
audiences.approach: Keep it concrete and short. Use the chair and the heap; get agreement that the chair can't hold itself together and that its holding-together is happening now. Then state the principle precisely: things with parts need something uniting them. Let them raise ‘What caused God?’ and show that the principle's own wording answers it — only what has parts needs a cause. Save the attributes for once the first stage is accepted.
audiences.openingQuestion: If I took your phone apart and laid every piece on the table, would you still have a phone?
audiences.avoid: Don't unload Aristotelian jargon (form, matter, act, potency) at the start, and don't call their objections stupid even if Feser calls them ‘incompetent’.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So the argument is: the chair has parts, therefore God? That's quite a leap.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: There are steps in between. First one: would the chair exist if its legs, seat, and screws were piled in the corner?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: No. You'd have chair parts, not a chair.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: So the chair exists only while its parts are united. And the chair can't be what unites them, since there's no chair unless they're already united. Something else does it — screws, friction, molecular bonds, even the room staying cool enough.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sure, physics. Electromagnetic forces hold the molecules together. No God needed there.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Agreed, at that level. But the molecules, the atoms, the fields, and the laws governing them all have structure too. If it's a law that A and B combine, then A, B, and that law are a new package whose unity needs explaining. Physics tells us how each level holds; it never gives us something with nothing to hold together.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Why not just say it's turtles all the way down? An infinite regress of explanations.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because each level only has borrowed holding-power. It's like a stick moving a stone: the stick does it only because a hand moves the stick. Making the stick infinitely long doesn't give it power of its own. Without a source that isn't borrowed, nothing holds.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, but this is about the past, right? And cosmologists don't agree the universe had a beginning.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It's not about the past at all. Even a chair that existed forever would need its parts united right now. The regress goes down, not back. The argument works whether or not the universe had a beginning.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay. Then maybe the unity of the parts is just a brute fact. Some things don't have explanations.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then you haven't offered an alternative explanation; you've offered none. And I've given an explanation — something simple unites them. ‘Maybe there's no explanation’ isn't a reason to reject one that's on the table.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what explains your simple thing? What caused God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The principle was never ‘everything has a cause’. It's ‘whatever has parts needs a cause of their union’. Something with no parts has nothing to be united. It doesn't just lack a cause; it couldn't have one.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient. Why not say the fundamental particles are the partless things? Electrons don't have smaller parts.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: No smaller pieces, but they have a definite nature — mass, charge, spin — that's distinct from the fact that they exist. They could fail to exist. They're in some states and could be in others. That's composition too: what it is plus that it is, what it is plus what it could be.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Suppose I grant a simple first cause. Why think it's one, let alone God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Two simple causes would have to differ somehow — one has a feature the other lacks. But then each would be ‘simple cause plus a feature’, which is composite. So there's only one. It can't change, since change is gaining or losing a feature. It isn't material, since matter has parts.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And ‘mind’? That sounds smuggled in.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: By elimination. Abstract things like numbers can't cause anything; material things have parts; a thought depends on a thinker. The ultimate cause is none of those, so it's a mind, or more like a mind than anything else. Feser also backs this with the principle that a cause must somehow possess what it produces.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: But now you've given it power, intellect, goodness, eternity. That's a lot of parts for a partless thing.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Different descriptions, same reality — like ‘the morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ both naming Venus. And the words apply analogically: God's ‘power’ isn't a separate module the way ours is. In him, power and intellect are one reality seen from different angles.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That's close to incomprehensible.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It's hard to comprehend, yes. So is wave–particle duality, and for a similar reason: we're stretching everyday concepts to a domain far from everyday life. If an argument reached the ground of all reality and the result felt ordinary, that would be the suspicious thing.

socratic: If I took every part of your chair and piled them in the corner, would you still have a chair? What exactly would be missing?
Did your heart, lungs, and eyes exist first and then get assembled into you? If not, does that make you any less dependent on them being united?
If a chair had existed forever, would it still need its legs attached right now?
Can the chair be what holds its own legs on, if the chair exists only because its legs are on?
If glue holds two boards together, what holds the glue to the boards — and what holds the glue itself together?
When physics explains why atoms bond, does it ever appeal to something that has no structure, no parts, and no specific values?
Could there be two things if there were absolutely nothing true of one that wasn't true of the other?
If something can change, is there a difference within it between what it is and what it gains or loses?
Can a pattern — the shape of a stone, considered by itself — break a window?
Does ‘the morning star’ mean the same as ‘the evening star’? Do they name the same thing?
When you say the wine is good and your friend is good, are you using ‘good’ in exactly the same way? In a completely unrelated way?
If a thing could have failed to exist, is there a difference between what it is and the fact that it is?
If you explain why two particles stick together by citing a law, what would you say if I asked why that law holds rather than some other one?
Can something with no parts fall apart? Can it be assembled? What would it even mean to cause it?

traps.trap: Presenting it as a ‘first cause long ago’ argument, inviting the Big Bang and ‘eternal universe’ reply.
traps.fix: Say ‘right now’ early and often. Use the eternal chair: even if it always existed, it depends on its parts being united at this moment.

traps.trap: Stating the principle as ‘everything has a cause’.
traps.fix: State it exactly: whatever is composite needs a cause of its composition. Then ‘What caused God?’ answers itself.

traps.trap: Using only Lego-style physical parts, so the listener says ‘quarks are the simple things’.
traps.fix: Introduce metaphysical composition before they get there: even a partless particle has a nature distinct from its existence and potentials distinct from its actual state.

traps.trap: Opening with heavy Aristotelian jargon (form, prime matter, act, potency).
traps.fix: Begin with the chair and the heap. Feser himself says nothing rides on accepting the Aristotelian or Thomistic analysis; bring it in only when needed.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there's a simple first cause’ and leaving the ‘why call it God?’ gap open.
traps.fix: Run at least the headline Stage 2 derivations: unique (no differentiating feature), changeless, eternal, immaterial, a mind, purely actual.

traps.trap: Getting drawn into an abstract fight about the principle of sufficient reason when the listener says ‘brute fact’.
traps.fix: Make Feser's two-step point: a brute fact is not an alternative explanation but no explanation, and ‘maybe there's no explanation’ is not a reason to reject an explanation already on the table.

traps.trap: Overselling: claiming to understand exactly how God's attributes are identical.
traps.fix: Concede the mystery and explain why it is expected (the wave–particle analogy). The claim is that there is such a being, not that we comprehend it fully.

connections.note: The introduction sets the book's goal of showing that several independent lines of reasoning demonstrate the God of classical theism. Chapter 2 is the first place where that convergence is made explicit: the One and the Unmoved Mover turn out to be identical.

Chapter 2 leans on chapter 1 at three points: the per se (hierarchical) versus per accidens (linear) distinction and the argument that a hierarchical series must have a first member (step 7); the reasoning that the merely potential can do nothing (step 33); and the derivation of perfection, omnipotence, goodness, and omniscience from pure actuality via proportionate causality (step 35). Both proofs have parallel uniqueness arguments (differentiation requires something one has and another lacks), and both use the same replies to ‘What caused God?’, Hume, and quantum mechanics. They are two roads — act/potency and parts/whole — to one summit, since there can be only one purely actual being. Note also that form/matter and actuality/potentiality are themselves compositions, so chapter 1's world of changing things is a world of composites.

Step 23 — abstract objects are causally inert — foreshadows the Augustinian proof, which argues that abstract objects such as numbers and universals must exist in a divine intellect. Plotinus's placing of the Forms in Intellect, just below the One, is part of the Neo-Platonic background Augustine inherited.

The essence/existence distinction, introduced here as one kind of metaphysical part, becomes the foundation of the Thomistic proof. Chapter 4 can be read as a specialized version of this chapter's argument: things whose essence is distinct from their existence need a cause whose essence just is existence itself, in which there is no such composition. Its uniqueness argument (two such beings would each be existence itself plus some differentiator) mirrors steps 10–13 here.
The ‘brute fact’ objection and Gerson's reply depend on the demand for explanation; the Rationalist proof of chapter 5 defends that demand directly through the principle of sufficient reason.

Chapter 2 is the first substantial treatment of divine simplicity, which chapter 6 develops as the core of classical theism. There Feser shows that God's unity and his status as First Cause are inseparable from his simplicity (a composite God would need a cause and could have rivals — a mere ‘superangel’), expands the account of analogical predication and the principle of proportionate causality, and answers Plantinga's objection that simplicity makes God a property or abstract object. The sense/reference and analogy replies sketched in chapter 2 are the seeds of that defense.

The attributes that chapter 2 derives quickly — intellect, omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, and God's role as the sustaining cause of everything here and now — receive full treatment in the second half of chapter 6, including divine conservation, which is exactly the here-and-now dependence this proof relies on.

Chapter 7 confronts popular objections head-on: ‘What caused God?’ and the suggestion that the universe, the Big Bang, a multiverse, or the laws of physics could be the uncaused terminus. Feser explicitly applies the Neo-Platonic reasoning there: such things are composite, so they cannot be uncaused.

Chapter 7's discussion of what laws of nature are (mere regularities, Platonic entities, or descriptions of how natures behave) completes the reply begun in chapter 2's final objection: on no account can laws explain composition without presupposing it.

For the capstone, the Neo-Platonic proof is often the most intuitive entry point and the clearest illustration of why the First Cause needs no cause. Pair it with the Aristotelian proof to show convergence, and with the divine-simplicity material to show what kind of God the proofs reach.

quiz.q: What observation does the Neo-Platonic proof begin from?
options: That things change from potential to actual
That abstract truths such as mathematical ones exist
That the things of our experience are made of parts
